div.head: WOMEN'S GHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S GHAT.

The Royal Siriterse—The Queen had some -idea of going to the Isle of Wight after her recent severe cold. : Sir Dighton Probyn made several visits to Barton Manor, where preparations were being made with this object in view, but her Majesty is so much better, and ziaturally wishes to be as much as possible with her sisteret he Empress Marie of Russia, that she had aban- doned the projected visit. The King's House on Barton Manor stands about mid-way between Whippingham end Osbourn House, and was put in readiness not only for the Queen but also for the visit of the Prince and Princess of Wales during the sporis to be held at Osborne College next week. The Queen and the Empress Dowager Marie have been passing the time very quietly at Buckingham Palace, bat they have been out 'frequently, driving in the Park, attired in black and with n any furs. Concerning Dancing.—The King is said to favour tie an re stately dances; such as the minuet, and pavane, and there is some possibility of these "measures " finding a place in the Court hall programmes this sear. In his younger days the Ring was devoted to waltzing, but it .is rarely now his Majesty 'even walks througha quadrille. The Prince of • Wales has never cared for dancing, but, the Princes of Wales is very fond of the exercise, and the young Princess Mary is already a most energetic and graceful dancer. An Action in the "Lark Continent."—Miss Decima Moore, who made her debut in "The Gondoliers' in 1879, and afterwards took many leading parts in musical comedy, is the joint author w ith her husband, Major F. 0. Guggisberg, C.M.G., R.E., of an interesting hook of travel entitled " We Two in West Africa" publishedhy Mr. Heinemann—Miss Mnore's book relates to certain travels she undertook with ber husOand in Connection with the survey of a part of the Gold Coasts and Ashanti, and whilst it is amusing in many details it conveys a very clear idea of the condit'ons of lite in West Africa. Although the European has invaded the country with his roads' railways and mines, the -ways of the natives reinain much as they always we re. 'There is no feminist movement in West .Africa, and in the up-country %illageS Mies Moo:e says the men "just sit about all daY, and gossip" whilst the women have to do all the work on the farms, and the domestic drudgery. A wife costs about £4, ead as the men can earn money more easily than in the old times by working for the European, they can more freely indulge in excellent investments of this kind, and ex-President Rcosevelt's maxim thet " the life that is worth' living "is Worth werkiog for " finds no eeho amongst the " lords of creation in West Africa. Feminine Workers.—Miss Elizabeth Robins, in the course of a recent lecture on " Shall women Work ? " .told a story about a certain learned man of science, who opposed the reminist movement on the ground that with freedom and independence, women would not marry—" they will prefer to enjoy .themselyes." There could --"nuly be a viorse indict,utent of marriage and doe, --,t; tie- life, which was the idea of women's prore aenere. As to whether woman shall work, that tieeluestion which seems to have teen "fettled by the eees that there are already nearly six million women -workers in the country, if we include the two millions employed as domestic servants. Nearly one million are engaged in the textile industries a similar number in dressmaking, while there are 200,000 women teachers, 100,000 employed in firming, besides large numbers in the various professional classes. These figures suggest that no inconsiderable part of the nation's work is done by women, although, as the suffragists say, they have no ,voice in determining the conditions under which it is carried on. The Anti-Suffragist Movement.—The petition pre- sented to the House of Commons the other day in opposition to Women's Suit, ago, was got up by the Women's Anti-Sul/rage League, of which the Countess of Jersey is chairman. It is over three years since the militant suffragists began their organised agitation, and since October, 1905, they have endured nearly 350 terms of imprisionn,ent amounting altogether te a perioi of close upon twenty-five years. the "Anti's" have been more leisurely in their operations, but they bops to show Parliament that woreen do not, as a whole ask for the vote, and further petitlone are to be pro- sated to the House of Commons to this effect. Regarding Stationery.—Many novelties are offered ne from tinth to time in the s' ationery world, but the w envelope which folds over on to the front right band corner' and is there fastened down by means of the stamp, ntly be said to take front rank in this direction. The idea has little to recommend it and women of good teste will cling to the old-fashioned gummed envelope, and white or cream stationery instead of those-highly- •eolou. ed varieties that from time to time are placed -upon the market. The Hand-Bag.—When pockets were first denied us we flew to the purse with a handle. Leter ee increesed the size of the parse until it became 'a bag, and since then the bag has gone on growing in dimensions until' now the most fashionable specimens are about twelve inches wide, and ten in depth. The most desirable perhaps are those in plain 'miler with fittings and fastenings to match, and such bags are carried in the arms—much • the same as a pet dog would be—arid as though the handles did not exist. An Awkward Mode.—Camisoles are to be fastened at
the back, leading 'tailors aid dressmakers _objecting to

fit gowns over a row of buttons down the front. Need- less to say this decree on the part of Dame Fashion aids a new stumbling block to dressing, and life promises to grow more and more difficult to the ivoold-be modish individual, who is mfnus, R maid. The all-over embroidered camisole with puffed sleeves is likely to find the greatest favour, us summer advances—for wear beateate filmy lace-inserted muslin and art blouses. Only "One Eye Worn."—The mannequin who tilled an inverted " flower-pot " null one eye was entirely obscured, and then calmly assured the astonished customer that "only one eye to 'be worn this season," would appeat to posse's considerable triginality. At the moment one notes, at smart gatherings and in fashionable thoroughfares many curiong frcaks in millinery', but the "one eye" mode is certainly among the mosludicrons ever known of the recorded. Afternoon Bridge.—The craze for afternoon bridge is decidedly on the wane, which is perhaps a good thing for all concerned, especially those families in which the member responsible for seeing the household machin3ry runs upon oilel wheels, happens to be smitten with the game. Apart hem stakes, or the expense of "prizes" there is no doubt that afternoon blidee has proved very costly in the long run to middle-class women. Few comparatively among housewives, even though they possess good servants, can leave their homes regularly after lunch every day, end waste all the Lours lefore dinner, without paying d,arly for such procedure, and surely young girls could be better and more healthily employed. It is put forward by devotees of the game that the abolition of afternoon Bridge only means a return to gossip and scandal, but as a matter of fact plenty of this sort of thieg goes on during pauses in the game—the pauses being frequent when women only are concerned—and while tea is in progress, such opportuni- ties far outweighing those presented during an ordinary afternoon call. No one would deny the bard working-

housewife an occasional afternoon at cards, but those. -.responsible for the well-being of a home should count their linen cupboard', mending and, re-making basket, and general look-round, also outdoor exeree, all of which cannot well be crammed into the mothing hours, as coming before mere waste of titre, and those who have no homes or children to lock after ani care for, should surely find work of some desci iption cirry out, for folks less fortunate than themselves. MADGE.

COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING. Mr. Harold Gray's Final Reply. In concluding his first article, Mr. Townroe promised to consider objections to the proposals of the National Service League, and accordingly, one could reasonably expect to find in his reply a detailed examination of these objections. Granting that he laboured under considerable limitations of space, I think he could have made some contribution to this end, had he been willing. As it is, his summing up is mainly a reiteration of the proposals of the League, intermingled with a cynical disregard for Peace and contempt for those mavements which he flippantly calls" International Nonsense," In the first place, he complains that I have not seriously weighed their proposal to improve the physique of the nation,because I. made the statement "that physical development is merely subsidiary to the military, issue," implying that in their eyes militarism as generally conceived, came before physical development. Let me assure Mr. Townroe and his friends that I do not in the least doubt their sincerity in this matter of physical develop- ment. It would ill become me to think or act other- wise. What I mean to imply is that the League is first and foremost, a military association, and that physical development is simply a means to an end,and not an end in itself. Ido not question thh, military drill is capable of doing much good in this respect. But it was pointed out in my first article that in all real educational schemes the physical well-being of our children is a prime consideration. It is nothing short of audacity for our friends to assert that without shooting and rifle drill. &c., physical exercises are far from satisfactory. Physical degeneration is the result of a variety of causes, aml many remedies will have to be applied before a substantial improvement can be made. Will Mr. Townroeconfidently state that he has made out his case concerning the physical value of military training? Where are his facts? He somehow forgets that doctors disagree and he surely cannot instance the soldiers themselves. One readily admits that _drill smartens their appearance But these are picked men and under most circumstances would have remained sound. Again, he cannot say that inherent viciousness or even contracted viciousness is improved by military service. And is he sure that conscription will stop physical degeneracy? No, a thousand times no! For apart from inherent tendencies in the majority of cases, the very seeds of such degeneracy are set in the earliest years and certainly before the age of 18 and, no amount of military pirouetting will check it, for should think Mr. Townroe knows that such improve- ment is an affair of the mind. Mr. Townroe quotes Surgeon-General Keogh, who says in the latter part of his statement, that he regards medical training as physical training and as the finest thing for the race and for future generations? Did I say anything to the contrary? I said that physical training was the, primal consideration in our present scheme of. educa- tion and I may add, likely to become more so in the future, vide the new regulations of the Board of Education concerning Infants' schools. Such training is based on the finest medical, psychological and educational evidence, and granted political endeavours can be directed towards social cleansing, and less to war scares it, with its accom- panying - educational efforts, will make for us a finer and healthier citizen than any military conscription and provide the surest bulwark against invasion. From this, we are assured that educational efforts are directed against the prevention of degeneracy, and as the medical evidence is per- fectly conclusive on the point, why is there a need of a military conscription scheme for our youths? Thus it is we have a scheme, perfect, compulsory, embracing all the benefits- desired by Mr. Townroe and his friends on the physical side but with none of the features of militarism, On 'which Mr. Townroe and myself differ essentially. I much prefer the spirit that has created Bournville and the example it has set before us in this matter, than trust to the effects of the proposals Of the National Service League. i The truth s, that behind the League there is an ulterior political object which aims at exciting patriotic- (?) enthusiasu and encouraging the martial spirit among our boys and youths. Let us have first things first. The remarks under the head of the " Invasion Problem" are practically a summary of his second article, and he has not made the slightest effort to anuer the -questions 1 raimeti. Undcr thee conditions I may be pardoned if I re-state some of them.
2 FoLneysTZY McDOUGALL'S eaterit SELF—RAISING FLOUR The Examiner. Saturday, March 27, 1909.

div.head: QUESTIONS UNANSWERED
div.p: QUESTIONS UNANSWERED

(1) Is not all this fuss produced by the foolish jealousies of small, yet noisy and powerful naval and military factions in this country and Germany? And I may add further, the malign influence of the Yellow Press.

div.head: (2) Did not we lead the way in Naval Rivalry?
div.p: (2) Did not we lead the way in Naval Rivalry?
3) Where is the semblance of a quarrel betwixi the people of Germany, and the people of our own country ?

(4) Would Mr. Townroe be good enough to tell us of the good that would accrue, if this country fought and beat Germany? (5) Is it possible for us to finance a Navy at a little more than a Two-Power standard- whatever this phrase may mean and a conscriptionist Army? (6) What guarantee can he give that this citizen army will only be utilised for purposes of home defence? These are some of the questions haphazardly taken from my articles which Mr. Townroe declines to answer. No references of any kind are made to any one of them. -

It seems a little strange that the above questions should drop down from the clouds ,and that this philosophic idealism shoidd.be conveited, into hard, stubborn things. One wonders why 111- Townroe who is so practical, and who recognizes he is living in a matter-of-fact world, should not see_ these things. _ _

His references to Internationalism and Federation, are unworthy of the ideas he sets out to ridicule. Mr. -Townrne must be very ignorant of the character of the work that has already been accomplished .in these directions. In the first place, to .confuse what I termed " Inter-dependableness of peoples" with " Epicureanism," neither reveals knowledge of the subject nor sobriety of judgment. To the Epicureans man stands alone, and only occasionally does he edme into relation with his fellows. But such connections are accidental and momentary. Social obligations- are non-existent. The individual man becomes the centre of the universe. Man's salvation is reached through self-isolation. Epicurus himself lived in retirement at Athens,for the State counted for nothing. Surely then, there is a difference and a vital one too. Doubtless Mr. Townroe means to silence me by the wisdom of the ancients, for it i somewhat imposing and not a little terrifying, to be confronted with the respective philosophies of Plato and Aristotle. It is philosophy this time and not poetry. - But did these intellectual giants revolt in the manner indicated ? The philosophy of Plato was essentially social, recognizing _that virtue sprang from interest in socialised good. Aristotle teaches that the real end of morality lies in the pursuit of this goodness for its own sake and that society affords the necessary °pi-Kir- tunities for , well-doing. For the life that is thus enriched is not merely yours,mine,but also that of the neighbours among wilt= we -move. Even Socrates, their illustrious predecessor, was' once asked to what city he belonged. He replied "Neither to Athens nor Corinth, but to the Universe." The master-,stroke of their philosophy was to have discovered that men were moral beings that only men could be such, and that they could achieve advance, in their ethical vocation only by co-operating with one another in society. I fail to see how the individuals, comprising communities, who have voluntarily joined themselves together on a common basis, are . cramped in their ,services to their own home and country. Perhaps I may be allowed to quote what I said in Article 2, in order to forestall this type of objection.

"We do not. forget our home, because we care for the city, nor ortr own city because we care for the country, neither do we forgot the true interests of our country when we desire to co-Operate with other nations." Peace advocacy and endorsement of the same

communal policy between nations, by no means imply a want of good feeling and disregard of the true interests of thee at. home. To assert the contrary, is to postulate a false doctrine of divided affections, which does not square with experience. Mr. Townroe seems to imagine that such a consummation would produce a dull uniformity, a swamping of national characteristics. 'Wherever this broadening policy has been at work, say in Great Britain or United States of America, I do not know of any deteriora- tion in the value of those. particular traits of character in those sections which contribute to the life of the whole. I am, curiously enough, accused of disregarding the working out of the salva- tion and destiny of each State, like e;.ch individual, because I supported the idea to federate Europe: And yet, strange to say, one of the ' prominent features of my second article, was the emphasis I laid on the necessity of each individual realizing the importance of his individual responsibility, especially moral, and surely this is equivalent to.the working out of a man's salvation and destiny. Also, I added, that by a pro- cess of federation, States could best develop along their own lines, Which is radically different from the , Imperialism Mr. Townroe refers to, because there is ever , consequent upon the policy of the latter, an attempt at absorption or assimilation of other States. which is usually unsuccessful. and gives rise to Con- stant friction.

I agree with Mr. Townroe that we tare dealing with a tough old world, which is not Moved too frequently by altruistic motives. Selfishness in its manifold forms, ignorance, blind tradition and prejudice, are powerful influences to reckon with, and I have no • desire to hail "Peace" where there is no "Peace." Above all things I desire to be truthful in perspective. And for this reason I very much regret that he has had nothing to say frith regard to the progress that can now be happily recorded as having been achieved in the sphere of individual conduct, in relation to the application of arbitration to individual disputes. He says Law by itself is not enough. Behind the magistrates' • verdict is the policeman's truncheon." He continues "Behind a Foreign Minister is an Army." He imagines these are parallel cases. What a parody of the truth. Policemen likened to soldiers! The policemen's duty is to bring the wrong-doer within the range of justice. And punishment is weer administered until the accused is proved guilty.

Invariably in the soldier's case, the reverse pro- cedure is adopted. His work is to kill, at the behest of his rulers, without any reference to the justice of the case. In preparation for this work of slaughter, Mr. Townroe mentions in his first article about the boy enjoying military training, and declaring it to be one of the jolliest times in his life. Support is giVen to this by a quotation from-Mr. Hilaire Beiloc, M.P., in the same strain. These instances might be innumer- ably multiplied, but they would make no difference whatever to my position, which Mr, Townroe does not seem to understand. I know quite well that camp life is enjoyable to many young men, and its physical advantages considerable. But ' camp ' is simply- looked upon as a holiday, and therein consists much of the mischief ; because it faithfully reflects the painful fact that the moral issues in relation to them- selves have not been thoughtfully considered. Camp' stands for something novel; and akin to harmless adventure. Of course, this is another " washy" doctrine, but nevertheless it is an important one, and considerable interest would have been added to this discussion, had Mr. Townroe faced this ques- tion... It is a conspicuous example of "dribbling. the

ball" off the main- ground. - - Let me state most clearly that in everything I have ' said with regard to soldiering, that I have not in any way impugned the honour and integrity of our soldiers. Many of them are disinterested, brave and .self-sacrificing. They mean well and so far my admiration is sincere. - But that is no reason why I should close my eyes to the fact that they are "'misguided enthusiasts "and slaves to an abominable System. My hope is in the democracy, for the bulk of the people are peacefully inclined.' This War-god is enthroned by - small rival sections only, and for huge multitudes of innocent people to be" drawn " into this qulrrel would be the greatest disaster of the 20th century. Throughout my articles I have endeavoured to deal with principles: My concern, for the moment—for much remains yet to be said— is not whether-Mr. Haldane's calculations are too low or too high, or whether eight Dreadnoughts.shoidd be commissioned now, instead of four, etc., etc., but whether the respective democracies have, common- sense enough to see the futility of war and the reasonableness and equity of the desire for closer rela tiono.Govornments• eau a much „as well as diplomacy and Hague conferences, but the issues rest with the .people, were they wise enough to see them. Mr. Townroe s good-humoured banter and amusing metaphors at my expense, I greatly enjoyed. His wit and racy style, with a popular presentment of his

. ~ case, have made this correspondence interesting, and, „I trust,. profitable, for the issues of this momentous question are grave. I sincerely hope tha t his talents may some day be used in propagating worthier causes. Warrington. H. GRAY.

div.head: NEW BUFFALO.
div.p: A NEW BUFFALO.

Mr A H. Crosfield, M.P. Elected to the Royal Antediluvian Order. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, . M.P. for Warrington, was initiated a member of the "Samuel Wakefield" Lodge of the llo3al Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes on Tues- day night at the Midland Hotel, Warrington. There was a large attendance of the brethren from the Goldsn Fleece, Frederick Eonnell, and Victoi ia Lodges,and the ceremony of initiation was impressively performed by Bro. T. Walter Borlea, 1C.0.H., of Manchester, Past Grand Primo of England, assisted by Bro. Sam Gray, K.0.M., K.G.H' . Bro. V. 0. Wiles, K.0.M., K.G.H., and Bro. I. Goodwin, K.O.M. At the conclusicn of the ceremony Bro. BODES pro- posed the toast of " Our New Brother," and reminded Bro. Crosfield that both in the House of Lords and the Home of Commons they had enthusiastic members of their ancient and homAuable or.ler. Their. present Lord Chief Justice was an enthustic member of their order, and was actively associated with their orphanage. If they wanted any assistance with regard to any of their grievances they had a. strong body guard in Parliament,and in the last Parliament but one they Lad 117 memters of the order. (Applause). Bro. I3oden also alluded to the excellent work which was per- formed, not only on Letialf of the widows and orphans of members, but also on behalf of poor children, many thousands of whom were fed through the kindness of members of the order. In ccnclusion, Bro., Boden said be %las sure Bro. Crosfield would he 'pleased to help Buffaloism to the extent of his power. (Applause). . . .
The toast was drunk with nuisical honOtti4. MR. CROSFIELD AND THE.FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

Mr. CROSFIELD who, on rising to respond, had a most hearty reception, thanked•the. brethren most sincerely for the kind way they had drunk his health, and also Bro. Boden for the manner in which he had proposed it, and the interesting address he had given. Ile remarked that the p: °ceders to him was most interesting and he was delighted to bear that be would Le able to exchauge the greetings which had been explained to him with quite a number of friends in the House of Commons. He was further delighted to see and hear the absolute impartiality with which they had selected their mem- bers. (Hear, bear.) No party prejtelicts—(Applause) —but Food Buffs all round on the Conservative and Liberal side alike. (Applause.) A very happy sii.n it was and he said it was all seriott3ness,of the good feeling that underlay the broad, public national spirit which they would find in all England. (Applause.) They bad members, not only in the House of Commons, but in the House of Lords, and he was delighted to hear of the distinguished gentlemen who belonged to their ancient and honourable Order. They had men of great experi- ence connected with the Order and also other Orders who could give them all the assistance that they needed when any measure was to come before Parliament. (Applause.) As one of the newest brothers in this Order he would like to take the opportunity of saying that if at any time a little spade work was required he would be ready to do it willingly. (Applause.) He appreciated the privilege of joining the brotherhood all the more because of its practical ntility. The way the orphanage was maintained was the kind of thing that appealed in a very special manner to Englishmen, because it was a kind of that voluntary effort which was such a fcature in their national life,. end which was of such incalculable value to old Eng- land. By that kind of cuatom a man who needed a change of air to pull him through got a chance, if he was a member and had fulfilled his duties, and the helping hand V at was lent to the widow and children, were such thitgs that must appeal to an Englishman. (Hear, bear). • Besides its utility be ventured to think, whether Libe!al or Conservative, they would value the Order because it was ancient. When they looked back' upon the traditions of_ Old England which were rooted in our past history of national life,t hey did value those old landmarks in their history, and u hen he beard Bro. Boden quote ,Queen Elhabeth, and the Magna 'Charter he felt deeply the privileges he had had of joining this Order. He was vk.s, grateful indeed to them for their great cord'ality ad the admirable address given by Bro. Boden. (Applause). Bro. HowEs proposed the toast of " Our Visitors " and remarked that they all appreciated the kindness of Bro. Boden, and the ether visiting brethren who had graced the ledge with their presence. It was only by such interchange of visits as these that they kept in touch wall one another. (Hear, hear). • The teast was heartily drunk. Bros. SAM GRAY, BODEN, WILES and Gocinwmt responded. The remainder of the evening was spent in a very enjoyable manner, Ur) contributors to an admirable musical programme being Bros. W. Critchley, P. Smith and W. Sutton.

div.head: WARRINGTON A "FOREIGN POWER." Stockton Heath Against Amalgamatlen.
div.p: WARRINGTON A "FOREIGN POWER." Stockton Heath Against Amalgamatlen.

" You hive had a Mile entertainment and I hope you are all satisfied" remarked Mr. H. J. Westbrook (chairman) in closing the Stockton Heath annual parish meeting on Monday evening. The observition was an apt commentary on the proceedings for, with the possible exception of the gentleman who enquired what was the diameter of the main sewer, everyone appeared to regard the affair more or less as a joke. Over an hour was pleasantly passed in discussing, for the most part, minor questions and the meeting seemed quite disappointed when it at length realized that all available topics hid been exhausted. The most impor- tant subject—that of seeking Urban powers or amalga- mation with the borough of Warrington—received but cursory attention at the meeting, but this was no doubt because the ground had been so well traversed in the report of the special committee—(Messrs. H. J. West- ! b. ook, J. W. Bouchier, J. H. Clarke, J. McDermid, and Frank Warburton) appointed by the Parish Council in accordance with the desire exprested at the last Parish meeting. Summar;sed, the findings of the committee were :

URBAN POWERS :—Your Committee have, to the best of their ability, carefully considered the various questions and matters involved, and are of the unanimous opinion that the circumstances have not sufficiently changed silica the Report of 1905, nor do the conditi as and cecessities yet exist to warrant the seek7ng of Urban Powers in the Parish. On the one side would come— I.—The administration under an Urban Council, including provision of its own offices and officials. Towards this there would be appropriated the .£169 now paid to the District Council. 2.—Costs of the Enquiry. 3.—The possible refusal of further use of the Union Hospitals (towards which we now con- tribute), and the consequent necessity to provide our own Ho,pitals. On the other side would come any benefit accruing from local government and sole control of our own affairs. It is only fair to ray that our Parish is in a much better position than it was some years ago, as our affairs are now more directly under-the con- trol of the Parochial Committee, and the District Council. appear to give us more consideration and more latitude in the conduct and management of matters affecting our Parish. AMALGAMATION :—As regards the second matter to be onnsidered, your Committee,,after full con- sideration of all the present circumstances, includ- ing the question of a differenti d rating for a certain number of years, are unanimoas in the con- clusion that no sufficient advantage would accrue to this Parish by its inclusion with the administra-

tive area of ale County Borough of Warrington. The Parish "Courcil had Lnanimously adopted the report and after a discussioi mainly concerned with the payment to the village fin) brigade of£L—which it transpired was not a" retaining fee" but the expense incidental to practices.--the parish meeting also approved it. 'ilia Chairman was unible t) state whether a delay in

obtaining Urt.an powers would entail heavier permaOent charges. He said it would probably depend on the trade union rate, for they could not tell whether they would be able to obtain things us cheap five years hence.

Tee Chairmln then spoke at length on matters of moment which had cropped up during • the past year. "Un .ccustorned as I am to public speaking " he remarked with native mode,ty "it was not ray intention to deliver any spee3b, hut my colleagues said some people would be very much disappointed if I did not do as my predecessirs bad done and give you a summary of the happenings in the parish during the past twelve months." Continuing he said they had had a year of quiet and beneficial work in the local government of that important parish. If he might use King's speech language, he should say " Our relations with the powers, both foreign and ' 'home are of the most cordial and harmonious kind"—the horns powers being the Cheshire County Council and the ' Runcorn Rural District Council and the foreign power the Warrington Corporation. The interests of the ratepayers of Stockton Heath and Warrington were often clashing— on the questions of the tram fare and the price of gas, for instance. Prima facie they in Stockton Heath were not enti led to have the same benefits as the ratepayers of Warrington but beneath the surf Ace a very good case might be made out for Stockton Heath, whereby she was entitled, if not exactly to the same terms as the ratepayers in the Borough, certainly to more generous terms than she now received, particularly in the matters to which he had alluded. • "With regsrd to the tram fares " declared the chair- ' man " we are penalized in having to pay the dearest fare of any route wh7ch the trams serve, and with regard to gas, we pay a higher rate than many of us consider we ought to pay blld that for gaa which we consider is not up to the standard it ought to be." Dealing with tram fares, the chairman said that owing to their guilelessness and their simple trust in the speken word of an official of the Warr.ngton Corpora- tion, they did not ask for a promise which was made to be put in writing ani consequently they were not able tri produce evidence of that promise. It was to the

effect that no greater fare than a penny should be charged lithe trains came into Stockton Heath, and it was chiefly on that ground that they were so persistent in their efforts to get the fare reduced to a legitimate and reasonable figure. Neither logical reasoning nor peaceful persuasion had sufficed to induce the Tram- ways committee to drop the fare or to arrange half- penny stages. Alluding to the price of gas, the chairman com- plained th it in the p rst thei interests of Stockton Heath were absolutely ignored or neglected, or it. would have been provided that when thr re was a reduction in the gas rate Stockton Heath, as being included in the monopolised area, ought to have the benefit of it. They were left with very little to bargain with in Stockton Heath, Warrington had the mcnopoly for the wafer and the gas but he wished to emphasise distinctly that there was one thing that Warrington would want from Stockton Heath, and that was the power to bring electricity into the district. He should always maintain that Warrington was not .to have a single monopoly more in that parish, unless Stockton Heath got a substantial quid pro quo. It was often s rid that many people resided in Stockton Heath to escape the rates of the Borough. How far that was true and how far it was peitinent to the question he would not stop to inquire, but Warrington ought not to forget that, Stockton Heath with its sandy soil, salubriors atmos- here and beautiful avenues of trees, Iv .s furnishing Warrington with its right lung and providing the workers of that town who had the good serve to live in the parish, away from the din of the town, with fresh air to strengthen their lungs and purify their hearts, and.enable them to csrry on the work of Warrington. Alluding to the erection of the new Council school, which is toprovide accommodation for 600 scholars and cost £9,688 3s. lOdsthe Cba'rman commended the public spirit of the landowners in opening out a new road and expressed the hope that the buildines to be erected thereon would be regulated and that there would be no dwellings with "Queen Ann fronts and Mary Ann backs." (Laughter.) Mr. Westbrcok referred to the new system which had been adopted in Stockton Heath of making roads of tarred macadam snd said they had it on good authority that that was a dust preventive. "1 dr n't know what we should do without the Ship Canal bridge," the Chairman continued. "It always furnishes us with something to talk about when we have nothing else. Some time ago the bridge, owing to a breakdown as we believe, was closed for about three hours." An effort was being made by the Parochial Committee to bring some pressure to bear on the Canal Company that they should provide some secondary means of access to Stockton Heath in case the bridge failed to perform its duty. He would not pass any opinion as to whether the company would fall in with the suggestion, but when the Ship Canal Act was passed somebody who represented Stockton Heath ought to have secn that a provision was inserted to deal with such a contingency. The Chairman concluded by commending the work of !peal organisations—not omitting the recently formed ornithological society which he hoped would be able to prevail upon some throssels and blackbirds to perch for a certain time each day in the spring on some of the beautiful trees provided by the Tree Planting Com- mittee. Then they would be able to regard Stockton Heath as approaching as rear the Garden of Eden as it was possible to get. (Laughter.) Then the discussion began. It opened with the question of the lighting of the swing bridge and drifted to such topics as the fastenings on ash-pit doors, the diameter of the main sewer, the "growing habit" of throwing cigar and cigarette ends and waste paper in the streets, the "hideous hoardings " near the canal' bridge, the prov:sion of a letter box in Ellesmere-road, and the introduction of new works in the district. Mr. Rose nointed out that the cost of the new school would work out at £l6 per head but other leading Education authorities estimated that a school could not be provided at less than £lO per head. The Chairman, in a general reply, said the Canal Com- pany could not be induced to light the roadway over the swing bridge, as they contended it would interfere with navigation. He did not know what was the diameter of the main sewer but ho had always been assured it was sufficient and would be for some time to take all the sewerage the parish was likely to send through it. Under a recant Act the Csuncil would have power to contribute to the cost of converting certain privies into a different system and the ratepayers might rely upon it that their representatives would be suffi- ciently up-to-date to dell with the matter. With regard to the suggested removal of the hoardings he thought it was and I.olvd u:ol fro adividen pin tof riew,and unti ce roehed that angelic state of liking the prospects of the country in preference to 2 s. d. he was afraid there was no hope of the removal or the hoardings. The Council had not received any application fo,r the erec- tion of new works in the parish. They were hardly in the position of the Corporation of Warrington, who had lands of their own, and applications would have to be made to individual landowners in the pyish. They had not heard of any allotments being required in Stockton Heath. Mr. Hallows said the Rural District Council had granted permission for the extensisn of Messrs. Cros- fields works at Walton.
The meeting Kissed a resolution asking tho Post- master of Warrington to provide a letter box in Ellesmere-road, and to arrange for a Sunday' collection from that box and also from the Red-lane box.

It has been said several times of late that War- rington have a chance of getting into the first four and thus contesting the championship of the League, but, personally, I can see no ground for such a state- ment. If Warrington win all their remaining matches, which they should do, as every one is at Wildersiiool, they will only reaeli a percentage of 6300 whereas Batley, the fourth club in the League, already stand at 74.07 and are not likely to fall much below this figure. Moreover there are eight clubs • between Warrington nod Batley, so that the Wirepullers are faced with an impossible task in reaching the first four this season. I am convinced that it is high time a more serious effort was made by the club to secure the championship of the League—if only to sustain the interest of the crowd to the end of the season. We have had a bitter experießce just lately of the paralysing effect on the " gates " which a defeat in the first round of the Cup brings in its train when there is no championship left to fight. for.

One of the most pleasing features of the League tournament this season is the triumph of go 2d football as played by the Wigan team. They stanino the rest of the Northern Union clubs to-day in pretty much the same relationship as Broughton Rangers did in 1900. At Oldham on Saturday the Central Park team were at the top of their form, and they quite deserved their victory by six points. It was the first defeat Oldham had met with at home for nearly three years, and this fact adds lustre to the Wigan men's great achieve- merit. The result places Halifax second on the list, and the chances are that Wigan and Halifax will now have choice of ground in the semi-finals. Halifax did Batley .a pion turn in beating 'Salford, and it nolt seems fairly certain that . the semi-finalists will be Wig,an, Halifax, Oldham, and Batley especially as the positions were not changed by Halifax's win at HUB. and Oldham's at Hunslet on Monday. .
The League table up to date is as follows: • For Agst _

Warrington will to-day have their first serious match at home since the Cup-tie. Swinton are the visitors and they should provide fairly easy victims. The glory of the famous Lions has long since departed and Warrington no longer view them as foes whom it will be difficult to overthrow. There has been a big .change in the fortunes of the Blues since the days of J. Valentine, R. Valentine, Dai Davies, and J. Lewis. The efforts of the Swinton managers to get players worthy of filling the vacancies have been attended with poor success. The present side has some young and promising players, but it looks like taking another year or two to 'make Swinton F.C. a really formidable combination.

The home club are indulging in, one or two justifiable experiments for to-day's match. Mclntyre will have his first trial with the seniors at full back, and I 'have • little doubt that he will justify his selection, though the young " Heathen " has a lot to learn before he can be reckoned in the same class as Tilley. He is endowed With all the qualifications for full bock play,. and his chief fault is that of most juniors--a tendency to rashness. The full back's first "duty is to be steady, and then to develop tbe higher arts of the game. ,Bradshaw has done so well of late--he got two tries at Barrow—that he merits further trial, and to-day Treharne will stand down for him._ Bradshaw, the " A " team forward, also gets a trial with the seniors, while Fish is re-instated on the left wing. O'Neill is absent owing to injury.

The Warrington teams is certainly a strong one, viz., Mclntyre, full back ; Fish, Dickenson, Taylor and Bradshaw,. threequarters ; Brooks and Jenkins, half- backs'; Thomas, Dowell, Slnigars, A. Boardman, Belton and. Bradshaw, forwards,

- The magnitude of Warripgton's win at Barrow was surprise to all. Twenty-six points to five was hand- some and indicates the class of play Warrington pro- duced. They were favoured with ideal conditions and the forwards early gaining the mastery, the lacks had day out. Boardman, Thomas and Shugars fairly scattered the opposition at times, while the handling of the backs Was brilliant. Jenkins, Brooks, Dickenson and." Taylor were altogether too good for Barrow's inexperienced men, and on the play the score might easily have been 117:1f as large again. Gifford, the international 'full back, was in anything but good form, and it would appear that he has had rather too much football this season.

I heartily congratulate .the " A " team on winning the Combination Championship once more. They only wanted one more point last Saturday, and by trouncing lace to the extent of 30 points to nil they made assurance doubly sure. Jordan, the "A " loam skipper played a grand game, and scored 3 tries. He has given the team a fine lead all the season and I am still of the opinion that he is the best all-round footballer in 'Warrington's second

div.head: Warrington's Big Win at Barrow. ,
div.p: Warrington's Big Win at Barrow. ,

The Worrington men made tho long journey to Barrow on Saturday, and though such men as Fisb, O'Neil, end Dowell were absent 'hay provedlar too strona for the Furm as team and scored a handsome victors. Beautiful weather pi evailed, but the gate would not exceed 2,000, a fact for %%Well the home club's poor record this season is largely rtspc Teams :—Wari ington : Tilley, back; Treharne, Dicienscn, Taylor, and Bradshaw, threequarter backs • , Brooks and Jenkins, bap-backs ; Thomas, Sbugars, A. Bradshaw, A.. Boardman, P. Boardman, and BAton, for- wards. Barrow: Clifford, Lack; Treloar, Dobson,. Maly and Sirett,threequarter tacks ; Kea in and Buns half-backs; Thompson, Morgan, Teasdale Brown, , Jardine snd Little, forwards. Referee, Mr. Prie:Aloy, Salford.

Warrington started with the sun in their faces, but early on showed an ability to get possession and handle the hall effectively. Jt:nkins got away in his own quarter and threw to Treharne, who raced three-quarters the length of the'field and scored behind the posts, for Thomas to goal. The Barrow forwards next got the better of some loose work. and a kick being chargei matters looked black for the " Wirepullers," -Tilley, however, got the sphere away, a huge punt placing War- rington aggressive. Taylor got well away from Brooks'apass, and taking the game to the line he Irinded on to A. Boardman, for that player to cross, Thomas adding his second goal. Dobscn took ridvantage of ft penalty to place a goal. Immediately after this the Warrington backs were seen to the greatest. advantage in a passing mot °meat, which quite bewildered the home side, but Mr. Priestley abludicated the final pass to Treliarne forward. Barrow rallied and combined play led up to Tteloar ecoeng. From this point until the interval, Wart ington forced matters, end after Brooks and Dickenson had effected a grelat, run, the way was made clear for'Bradshaw to score. Thomas kicked his third goal. Half-time : Wartington, three goals three tries (15 points) ; Barrow, one goal one try (five points). , Turning round Birrow were early called upon to adopt defensive tactics, Brooks midi a strong ' attempt to cross until challenged by Si-att. The ball was got away to the quarter flag., hut tla, respite was only momentary, for the i•all'was speedly whipped out to Dickenson. who raced through the home backs to score a grand try. This time Thomas missed the goal shot. A free kick to Barr-'w took the game into the Warrington territory, but it tits only there for a moment. Brooks took up the ball and, beating Gifford, was sailing 'away Icautifully for the line whera S'rett, with a splendid tackle, grasted him a foot from the line. Barrow were now havirta• to defend all they knew. The pressure was eased' by a free kick to Barrow, and half-way was reached, where a passing -movement was commenced by Jenkins. Bradshaw took the -hall from Taylor and dashed down the line. Giff.;rd failei to.t.ickle him and Bradshaiv scored iVarrington's fifth try. Some promising ,play by Dobson and Tteloar was spoiled by Tilley, but the following play favoured Barrow. A rush by Trehirne and Diettenswa came to grief after Jenkins scored a try. Thomas kicked .a goal. This closed the scoring. Result :—Warrington, four goals six-tries (26 points) ; Barrow, one goal one try (five points).

div.head: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. WIDNES.
div.p: BROUGHTON RANGERS v. WIDNES.

At Broughton, before 4 000 people. From the out- set it was seen that the Rangers were much the stronger ride, and only one minute had elapsed when Harris opened th 3 score with .peralty goal. A few minutes later Wright broke clean away,- and when faced by Jones gave the leather to llt,gg. who easily scored under the posts. Although the Widf.es for- wards were hating the btst of the serum- age they could not make much headway. Mottrara got over for Broughton', but Harris failed at goal. A determined 'effort by the Widnps si-ie resulted in Taylor sc,rines try and placing a erial. Close on the interval Ruddick registered a third try for the Ranger.?, which llarris improved, and at half-time Broughton lea by 15 points to 5.

In tie second half Widnes were quite outclassed, despite the fact that Broughton lacked the services of Wriot, who had retired injured. It was not long Lefote Hauls scored a N. -,t.le of trie?, ban of which i.e improved, while Mottram and Hogg also crossed, both trirs being converted by Harris. For Widnes, Carr crosfed the line in the last ndnute and Taylor placed a goal. Result :—Broughten Rangers G goals, 7 tiles (33 points). Widnes 2 gelds, 2 tries (10 points).

div.p: WARRINGTON "A" THE CHAMPIONS.

By their victory over Tne.e r.t Wilder,peel on Satur- day, Warrington " A "secured the championship of the Lancashire Combination. The visitors started s.nd Warrington quickly forced play into the Ince quarters, hut CunlitTe relieved a big kick, end Hockenbtell mark- ing, Mclntyre landed a splendid goal fron t he. touch. After this rtvetse the visitors pressed, hut the home defence proved sound. A round of.passing by the home backs ended in Jordan racing over at the corner, Mclntyre adding the goal. Just before the interval the same player again crossed, Mclntyre again converting. Half-time : Warrington "A," tuelvo points ; Ince, nil. In the second half Ince made a poor show against the home attack, and tries vre:e scored by Hockenhull. Cart wright,Jordpn, Harmer, the last two in particular being brilliant efforts, and Mclntyre improved_ thrce. Final : Warrington "Alsix goals six tries (0 points); Ince, nil.

div.p: THE ASSOCIATION GAME.
WARRINGTON " OBSERVER " CUP. FINAL.

SUTTON CON' 11F, C TAT, V. CLOCK FACE.—Great interest was taken in the struggle for this trophy on the Albions Ground, Liverpool-road, on Saturday, and there was an excellent attPhdanci.. D.aing the first half, exciting end to end play Vl ai the order, but no scoring took place. Turning round, disaster early befell Cock Face, for they soon lost the services of Lawrence,whilst another player was also carrie I off. With nine men, however, Clock Face forced the game at the Sutton end, and thrice the Sutton goal had tarrow escapes, Tajlor on one occasion turning a hall at full length on the ground. Both sides missed penalties, whilst near the close Sutton attacked strongly, but failed to beat the defence, and the result was a pointless draw.

The half-yeaily meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Bowling Association was held at the. Albion Hotel, Manchester, on Satw dig evening, Mr. J. W. G. Coombes presiding over a large attendance of memb9rs. A very satisfactory balance-sheet was pre- sented, the sum in hand being just over .£2O. Mr. A. II Crosfield, M.P., to whom a hearty vcte of thanks was passed for his services, was re-elected president. TOe remaining offit lids were appointed as follows :—Deptity President, Mr. J. W. G. Coombes; hon. secretary, Mr. C. Smith ; hon. trea-urer, Mr. W. H. Hindley. • Mr. 0. Leek was added to the Hsi, of patroi-s. The following clubs were admitted to membership of- the Association ;—Albion Club (Old Trafford), Bolton Griffin, Cris Ke3 s (Eccles), Wien Subscription Club, Radcliffe Withirs, Cadishead Social Club, Levrnshulme Midway, Chapel House (Heaton Chapel). Tie Association passed a resolution recognlsiog the schenic of , the British Crown Assc,ciaticn, whereby I y competition a Iliitisli Bowling Champion shall be acclaimed annually. The proposal was that the last eight men left in the annual Individual Merit Compe,i- -t ;ens of each of the counties, Lancashire and Ctiesnire, Yorkshire and Staffordshire, or any other counties affiliated, shall take put in this Annual Competition. The Comity Championships proposed for the ensuing year will be decided as follows 6th. .Stafford- shire v. Lant-ashire-; June 16th, Yorkshire, in Yodishiro, July 10th, Strlfordshire, in Stafferdshire ; July 2411, Yorkshire, in Lancashire. div.head: RAILWAY FATALITY AT PADGATE.
div.p: RAILWAY FATALITY AT PADGATE.
Old Lady Cut Down by Express.

The Cheshire Lines railway station at Padgate was the scene of a shockivg. fatality on Tuesday, the victim being Mrs. Cicely Oldfield (72), who lived at Locking Stumps Farm, Croft, about a mile and a half distant. The deceased, who was about to go to Warrington by train, was attempting to cross the line in the rear Of a stationary train, and failed to notice the approach of the ..1.30 express from Manchester, which hurled her twenty yards and knocked out her brains on the -bridge which carries the road over the station at this point. Both her arms were broken and one leg severed. •Deceased was carrying a small bag, which was contained in a larger bag, and while the latter was found near the body the small bag was found on the express engine when Warrington was reached, and she was identified by means of a cheque inside the bag. Mrs. Oldfield was very energetic and active in spite of her age and before starting out for Warrington had done her week's washing during the morning. She leaves four sons and one daughter, two of her sons being at present in America. She lived with the other sons at Croft. -
THE INQUEST. JURY'S RECOMMENDATION.

The inquest was held on Wednesday in the w3iting room at Padgate Station by Mr. A. Jones deputy coroner. Superintenderet Ramage represented. the C.L.C. Mr. Blackwell acted as foreman of the jury. William Oldfield, farmer, Croft siid that decease was his mother. She was 72 years of age and a married woman. She left home at 12.45 o'clock on Tuesday to go to Warrington by the 2 o'clock train from Padgafe Station. She was in her usual state of health' and was not bard of hearing. The deputy Coroner : Do you know why she crossed by tie crossing instead of using the road bridge,as thete is a booking office on the other side. The Foreman : Ihe booking office on the other side is an innovation. It is a matter of custom that passengers cross._
The-Deputy Co-oner : They bare been anctis- turned to go that way, and it is very difficult to get them out of it.
A Juror: It is a long way round by way of the briace. .
Witness continnin' e said that the bag (produced) containing cheque and hank hook, was in deceased's possession al the time amd wit* found on the foot board of the express at Wallington. _ -

George Lewis, goad, 76, :113rtle-street. Liverpool, said he was passenger guard of the 12.33 train from Liverpool, duo at l'adgate Station nt 1.40 o'clock. Witness was locking out of the window when he saw the deceased going down the slope at the end of he pia t form.
Ihe Foreman: Which side of the van were you look- ing _out of ? _ _ _

Witurss : The platform side. It was apparently her intention to cross round before the express was due. I shot.ted to her to keep bade, but sh seemed stunified and did not ply any attent'on, but went on. I did not, see her iteeeted down. Ste was behind my train. A Jt.ror : Why did you spent( to her. Witness, : Because I thonght she was in (longer. A Juror : Is it the custom for yon to do so ?

Witness : If T see ar.y danger I -tell them. William Choppell, 22, Ilf-lvoinstreet, Manchester, said he was the Oliver of the 1.:10 express from Manchester In Live Tool. lie entered qe station I,t a speed 61 50 miles pct hour, tl.e whistle was blowing at thd time. He SAW an elderly lady attempt to cross the line. She would then be two conch lengths any. He applied the brakes.hut it was too late. On looking on the other kide of the engine he taq the body or some part of the clothing under the train. He reported the -matter at ‘Varrington en his arrival. The Foreman : Where did Tot: commence to whi•-•Ic ? Witness : At the signal Los, before reaching the statical.
A Juror : There is n notice entsitle the stat:on thnt the spced must- not exceed 30 miles on hour.
The Forcman : Did you feel cny concussion on strik- ins, the body ? Witnrs3 : No.
A Juror: The presumption is that she was hastening to gPt o'd of the way. The Deputy C -ironer : Yes I think so. A.Jurer : Were you running to time. _
Witncs•s: 1 Oink T hlfamini,tp into at Warrington but it was accounted for, by applying the brakps.

William Disclrd Pollitt, carriage exa.rainer, in the employ of the eomnany at Warrington, said he examined the express train on its arrival at Warrington ani found the bar (prodneei) on the brake of one of the ca•riages at the rear of the train. The Foreman: I think it is rather wonderful that it shou'd have been carried on the footboard.

Darcrn Seddon, plate lacer, said he was working Ala SOO yards from the stat ion towards Warrington. He saw the deceased go round from behind the S'ONV train cud she was knocked down by the express. The hody was burled through the bridge and carried about 12 yards. P.C. Hsalli, stationed nt Padgate. said he found the boly sho,kingly mutilated at the Padget° Station bridge. He also found a leather bag containing a pair of spectacles and two pennips. The -Deputy Coroner: It seemed that the woman crossed the line t 9 escape going round by the bridge. She was evidently not aware of the danger. She as apparel:lly following out her ustrd custom. A Juror: She had a right to cross the lice bi the crossings._ •
The Deputy cproner : Hew do on make tLat out? Juror: It is :the usual enst,:an.

The Coroner: That may be hut she had no right. The Fol earn I think the object of the crossing simply to help the porter; and railway employe's. Mr. Ramage : That is al. A Juror: If we had a Lridge it would obviate the danger. The Deputy Coroner: Anotiaer bridge would not obviate the difficulty. _ _
A Juror : If they have no right to crcss, the pasFengers should be s'opped.• The Deputy Coroner: The Railway Compary could do that. _ _

_ Mr. F. Miginn (a juror) : T do not think one per rent of the people travelling from that station go by the foot bridge. The Deputy Coroner: T quite aeree. The Railway Company should prosecute all psnple who erroli the Ilne. There is a notice sign and I suppo....e people have read it. . . _ _ .
Mr. Magion : Et hris been the custom to take little not ice of those notices.

The Deputy-Coroner: The only effective way is to prosecute the people vk he cross the line by the way of the crossings. A Juror : The constructivn of the station gives every inducement for people to cross the line by way of the crossings,
_ The Depoty-Coroner : That may be sn ' but she could have got to tho other platform without crossing the lino at all.. She did this as a inatter of convenience.
- A Juror. There are a great many trains passinz d Lily and it is one of the most dangerous nighxays in England. In gly opinion we ought to have another bridee.

The Foreman: Spealing personally I do not. think that if a bridge were erected in the centre of the plat, rorm the prople would use it. Mr. Maginn : T sugge,t that the level croesing should be put. at the other enl of the platform and not near the bridge._
The Deputy-Coroner : If people cross the line they nftt‘t take the risk.

The Foreman : We are in the unfortunitte position that many of the trains for Warrington arrive at the same moment the express is etp. The Deputy-Coroner : That shows the danger, and therefore you ought to b; more caieful in crossing the line. 111r.Maginn : Personally I think that railmay compiny should come into the same line as manufacturers, and adopt. means in order to prevent accidents where they are likely to occur. The Doputy-Coroner : The railway company should prosecute every person who crosses the line. The jury returnei a verdict of " Accidental death," 2nd recommended that a new foot bridge should be erectel opposite the twain of:1e or in some-con- venient spot close by.

was the declaration of policy which it drew from Mr. Asquith. The Prime Minister said that, apart from the question Qf six, in regard to which the Government adhered to its declaredsattitude, the Government was -strongly in favour of a reform upon a wide reach of the existing franchise, the abolition of plural voting, . the disappearance of the artificial and illogical distinction between occupiers and lodgers, the material shortening of the period of qualification, and a thorough- going simplication of the machinery of registration. But the Prime Minister went on to add—as everyone with the slightest knowledge of constitutional Proetdure would anticipate—that any measure of this kind', if it is to take a place upon the Statute Book, should proceed from the responsible Govern- ment of the day, and should be carefully moulded in the stress of deliberate and pro- longed Parliamentary consideration.
• Sir Samuel Chisholm, LICENSING BRIBES the ex-Lord Provost of TO MAGISTRATES. Glasgow, has felt con-

strained to utter some grave words of warning concerning the shameless aggressions of,the drink trade and its daring attempts to establish a supremacy inimical to the public weal. With a full sense of the meaning of his words and speak- ing out of his own knowledge he said: " I know of a licensing magistrate whose views on the temperance question were Well known who was seriously asked by a prospective applicant for a license if he would take £2OO and take his holidays during the month of April, the month when the licensing court held its sittings. I know of another magistrate on whom an applicant for a 'license called canvassing for his vote. When the applicant left there was found on the desk an envelope addressed to the magistrate's wife and :E5O enclosed. I know of a publiCan who admitted that he had given £6OO that it might be divided amongst the members of a licensing bench for the purpose of influencing them to grant an apolica- tion for a license which he had made. The transaction would probably never have been. _ heard of, had the application been granted; but it was refused, and the publiean found that his money had' not been distributed and 'then he lodged a complaint. These cases, which are all within my own knowledge, might doubtless ' be multiplied indefinitely by others whose experi- ence may be wider than my own, but they are sufficient .to illustrate the deadly peril to 'which the purity and integrity of our own public life is exposed by the relation in which it stand ito the drink traffic."
The new Children's CHILDREN AND Act comes into force on

PUBLIC-HOUSES. Thursday next, and it is well that the general public should know something of the condi- tions it lays down relative to the serving of intoxicants to children and their presence at the bars of licensed premises. By the new law, the presence of a child under the age of fourteen years in any bar is entirely pro- hibited. It does not matter for"what pur- pose the child may be there, nor whether the child is alone or unattended. If a child under fourteen is found in the bar the licensee is held to have committed an offence, unless he can prove one of two things: (1) that he used due diligence to prevent the child being admitted, or (2) that the child was apparently over the age of fourteen. Parents or others, who take or send any child under the age to the bar of a licensed house, or who give to children under five years of age any intoxi- cating liquors without the sanction of a ,doctor are liable to a heavy fine. Upon these points the Act is clear and emphatic, and the general public can do good service in gin-ring vigilance and reporting any instances in which its provisions are transgressed. It will be noted that the Act does not apply to " off " license-holders, for where the sale is only for consumption off the premises there can be no bar under the meaning of the Act. All who help to spread a knowledge of this new law will help forward the cause of the children. It is a charter of reform and will emancipate the little ones from one of the most pernicious of influences. Women will no longer be able to carry their children into the tainted atmosphere of the public-house and there can be no doubt that this will have the effect of preventing to some extent the visits of the mothers themselves.

The Trade can hardly be expected to' take kindly to the new law, for it is part of the Licensing Bill of last year against which they railed' so vigorously. The most enterprising of liquor sellers propose to defeat the working of the Act by providing nurseries in which the children wal be cared for free of "charge while the parents are drinking—and perhaps getting drunk—in the bars. We do not think the experiment will be made even, if such a loophole can be found in the Act. English parents have inflicted shameful wrongs upon their children when their wits and moral sense have been blunted by alcohol, but we do not think that in their sober moments they will submit their children, even for entertainment, to the mercy of the publican._

div.p: i NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Mrs. Lloyd-George, who opened the Golden City Bazaar on Wednesday, charmed everyone by her pleasant and unostentatious manner and the delightful little_ speech with which she encouraged the workers. That homely touch about the familiar Welsh names which comfronted her in the bazaar literature was highly relished, a,nd her visit will always be recalled as a pleasant event in local annals. * * *

Everyone will be glad to hear that we are to have a new comic opera from the pen of Sir W. S. Giljaert. It is many years since he wrote the last of the Savoy operas, and it was hardly expected that he would again reappear in a field which he has made peculiarly his own. The music to the new opera is to be composed by Mr. Edward German, and it will, it is hoped, be produced towards the end of May. _ _

The Chancellor of the Exchequer intends to spend a portion of his Easter vacation in opening the golf course recently laid down near the new mansion which he is building for himself not far from his old home at Criccieth, in Carnarvonshire. Mr. Lloyd- George is an enthusiastic and, on the whole, successful golfer, is a member of the Walton Heath club, where he has for opponents Sir Joseph Lawrence and other ardent Tariff Reformers. * * *

Mr. A. H. Crosfield. -M.P., made a timely allusion to the naval scare in his speech at the Golden City bazaar on Wednesday. The member has had the advantage of consult- ing expert opinion and he was able to assure the timid ones not only that our defences are in a magnificent condition but that in 1912—that much-talked of year—we shall still be immeasurably superior at sea. As Mr. Crosfield tersely put it, the present manufactured agitation is"sadly and unfortu- nately exaggerated." * *

The Rev. John Wakeford, one of the Liberal clergy in the diocese of Liverpool, and one of the preachers of the Friday night addresses at the Parish Church, has this week been the luncheon-hour preacher at St. Paul's Cathedral. Mr. Wakeford succeeded the present Bishop of Norwich in the vicarage of St. Margaret's, Anfield, to which he was appointed by Mr. Gladstone, who had been much struck by some sermons he heard him preach when a comparatively unknown young clergyman at Brighton.

The actual spring equinox—the arrival of the sun's centre at the Equator and its entry into the Zodiacal sign Aries—almost exactly coincided this year with the rising of the sun on Sunday morning at Greenwich. Both last year and in 1907 we enjoyed brilliant sunshine for several- days preceding the equinox, though, curiously enough, the temperature was more suggestive of mid- winter; this year mild but cloudy weather ushered in the first day of spring. From Monday the sun moves northward, and in our latitudes the duration of possible sun- shine will increase rapidly, so that by the end of March the day will exceed the night by fifty minutes.

* * * Under a system of Free Trade we have reared in a narrow area a population which is necessarily dependent for its sugtenance upon sea-borne food supplies-; we have absorbed an immense proportion of fhe carry- ing trade of the world, and we have to a large extent become the world's bankers. Mr. Balfour asserts that it is possible to abolish the system which has made these developments possible, and yet not to cause' any "undue shock to national industry or the course of national trade." The onus of proof lies on those who make so startling an assertion. But Mr. Balfour, when we ask for his proof, only tells that Cobden objected to Factory Acts, and that Mr. Marshall admits that Protection may sometimes be useful in fostering infant industries.

The new Children's -Act, which comes into jorce next Thursday is very far-reaching in tis provisions, as may be judged from the fact that there are 134 sections, touching upon infant life protection, the provision of fire guards, juvenile smoking, and the exclu- sion of children from licensed premises. A vigorous effort will be made to stamp out smoking by youngsters and any person selling cigarettes &c., to a child apparently under sixteen years of age will be liable to a fine of £2 for the first offence, £5 for the second offence, and £lO for third and subsequent offences. Constables and park keepers are duthorised to. search any boy ap`parently under the specified age for the purpose of relieving him of tobacco, cigarettes &c. * * *

People do not always show a proper concern for the ethics of raising money, so long as the end is attained, and some remarks by the Bishop 'of Liverpool on the subject will, we hope, receive the attention they deserve :—" I would earnestly ask you to use the utmost care in the means you employ to raise money for religious purposes," said the Bishop to the clergy of his diocese the other day. "A sale of work, properly managed, may," he continued, "be a real blessing not only to the parish which needs funds but to those who work for it. But lotteries and raffles ought to be entirely forbidden. They help to foster the growing spirit of gambling which is one of he greatest curses of our people." * * *

Monday's message of the New York correspondent of the " Times" with refer- ence to the United States Tariff is especially interesting. For it is made clear that Great Britain will be in a better position than countries with a Protectionist tariff. The new tariff has maximum and minimum pro- visions, and Great Britain is entitled at once to the minimum rate, because we treat United States trade " with fairness and impartiality.,' "The maximum and mini- mum sections are causinc, anxiety to all the foreign Embassies and Legations except the British." We are alWays told that this country gets the worst of the deal because we have nothing to bargain with • yet here we have the United States fairly enough saying that we are entitled to the best treat- ,ment because we levy no protective duties on United States goods. This is an interest- ing and significant departure. * * *

The Tories have been doing their utmost to lash the nation into a state of panic with regard to our naval defences. Dr. Macnamara. the Secretary of the Admiralty. described the feeling of many people when in a speech at a men's meeting at Kennington on Sundays afternoon, he said he was getting a bit con- cerned about John Bull. Apparently now on the slightest provocation John Bull broke out into a cold sweat, and began to look like a person in an apopletic fit. Really. said Dr. Macnamara, our old friend was beginning to get a little jumpy. It was\true,that a great friendly State had recently made extra- ordinary efforts to equip rapidly a very powerful fleet—that was their business—
but to suggest that the supremacy of the seas would pass into the keeping of the director of that fleet was not clear to any impartial person who would examine the truth. ' * * *

The Rev. J. W.- Isherwood, who delivered special addresses to men and women at the Warrington Parish Church yesterday, is the son of one of our best known towns- men—Mr. Robert Isherwood, commission agent, Bramhall-street. He was born in "the good old town" and received his early education at People's College. Obtain- ing a scholarship, he went to the Boteler Grammar School for two years, and then proceeded to Owen's College, Manchester, where he ' obtained his M.A. degree. For two years he was engaged in teaching work in Germany and Switzerland, and returning to England,took the degree of L.Th. at Durham University. In 1896 he was ordained deacon at Worcester and in 1897 priest at Coventry. His first curacy was at Btomsgrove where he worked from 1896 to 1898. Since then he has held curacies at Kidderminster and Shrewsbury and is at present chaplain on a private estate at Berwick,_ near Shrewsbury.

Apropos of the libel action which Mr. Lloyd George was forced to take, it may be of interest to mention two previous similar actions in which the private character of famous politicians was affected. The last prominent politician who figured as plaintiff in a libel case was Mr. Parnell, whose action against the "Times," arising out of the Pigott forgeries, was settled without going into court for .E 5,000. tin the other case it was the private character of the defendant which was affected, the politician in this case being Mr. Disraeli (afterwards Lord Beacons- field), who in a speech in Buckinghamshire denounced CharleA Austin, a well-known Parliamentary counsel, in slanderous terms for having made mendacious statements under the protection of the robe he wore. In this the plaintiff instituted criminal inforrna- tion,and Disraeli, appearing in person,abjectly apologised, and he was fined heavily. "Dizzy" was so embittered after this against barristers for the rest of his life that he always referred to them disdainfully as "gentlemen of the long robe."

Personal. The results of examinations in the Faculty of Medicine at the University,. Liverpool, were reported to the Senate on Wednesday. Mr Sidney Tinsley, eldest son of Mr. William Tinsley, of Latchford, has obtained his final MB., Ch.B., Part 2, with honours in the second class.

Miss Hilda M. Stansfield, head prefect of Man- chester High School for Girls, and daughter of Mr. Mr. W. H. Stansfield, received intimation on Monday that she had won an open scholarship of £25 a yehr for thre years at St. Hugh's Hall, Oxford. The subject was modern history.

Chamber of Commerce. At the monthly meeting of the Chamber of Com- merce on Thursday, a resolution was passed which urged the London and North Western Railway Company to undertake the erection of a new station at Bank 101 uay as 'early as possible. The Council also passel a resolution in favour of the New Warrington Bridge being not less than 80 feet in width. Legacies to Local Institutions.

The late Archdeacon Blackburne, Rector of Bury, whose estate has been valued for probate purposes at £24,860, left sundry legacies, including £2OO each to St. Elphin's School, Darley Dale, and to the Institu- tion at Warrington for the Relief of Widows and Orphans of Clergymen. Corporation Surplus Lands. - -

Thomas Sutton and Sorts, on behalf of the Corporation, offered for sale certain surplus lands in Bridge-street, Koutsford-road and Liverpool-road, Warrington. Thera was a fair attendance but the bidding was very poor and all the lots were withdrawn. Wool) MANTELS, Kitchen Ranges and Tiles. Large stock. Estimates free.—J. S. Penny .Popular Concerts. The popularity of these concerts shows no signs of waning and on Saturday evening the Bold-street ,chool-room was filled to its utmost capacity. The Rev. T. Miller presided and delivered an address on the evils of drinking and gambling. The programme was an excellent one and all the performers were well received. The artistes were the Misses Davenport, Yates and Bancroft, and Messrs. Platt and Williams. The humorous element was well sustained bethy Bros. Cross.

" Le Domino Noir." In connection with the Manchester School of Music, "Le Domino Noir," Auber's grand opera in three atts, was produced last. eyening at the Midland Theatre and will again be performed this (Saturday) evening, in aid of the sustenation fund to assist specially talented but necessitous students. Miss Felicia Sutton, of Warrington, is taking the principal con- tralto part—" Jacintha." Mr. Ryder Boys, whose company visited Warrington last year, is the stage manager and coach. In concluding their report for the year ending 1908 the Committee of the Warrington Training College place on record their intense satisfaction that 1908 saw the comp!etion by the Principal of his 25th year of administration of the College, and that he continue to show abundant evidence of sound health andsigonr. From his inception of the onerous and responsible duties connected with the office, the history of the College has been one of marked progress in every direction; and the committee feel that to his sympa- thetic, tactful, earnest and most efficient supervision and personal influence, loyally supported by hls staff, is mainly due the high position reached and held by Warrington amongst the training colleges of this country.

The-marriage was solemnized at the Church of St. Michael's in the Hamlet, Liverpool, on Monday, of Mr. John Ta3lor .Sampson, of Grappenhall (late sccretary of the Warrington Cycling Club), youngest son of the late Mr. John Sampsqn, and Miss Mary Dowling, of St. James's-place,- Toxteth Park, Liver- pool, only daughter of the late Mr. F. Dowling. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. S. W. Payne. The bride, who was given away by her uncle, Mr. William Sampson, was very prettily attired. Mr. Fred Valentine, of Appleton, Widnes, acted as best man. Many useful present have been received by Mr. and Mrs. Sampson, as well as Feveral telegrams of con- gratulation. Tbe honeymoon is being spent in London.

Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds The quarterly meeting of members in connection with, the above Lodge was held at the house of Bro. James Gleave, Barley Mow Hotel on Saturday. A very creditable report of the pi st quarter's working was given by the Auditors P.M. William Taylor, and Bro. George Ratcliffe. The amount paid as sick benefit was £93 55., carrying forward the sum of £lB ss„ making the total worth of Lodge £2,317 9s. 9d. After the election of Lodge and District Officers, P,M. James Atkinson presented P.M. Arthur Parr with a framed ,Emblem of Merit for services rendered to the Lodge.

GARDEN TOOLS, Wire Netting, Roofing Felt, S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Death of Mrs Marson. ' Many Warrington people will regret to hear of the death of Mrs. Marson (widow of the late Mr. James Marson, J.P.' f rmerly of Hill Cliffe, Warrington and a' director of Peter Stubs, Ltd.), which took place at St. Leonard's-on-Sea on Sunday. The deceased lady, who bad attained the advanced age of SI years, resided when in this district in the house formerly occußied by the late Mr. Holbrook Gaskell and at present the residence of Mr. Henry Greenall. —The funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Wednesday. The body was brought by special train to London and thence, to Warrington (Bank Quay), and was interred in the family vault at the Cemetery at 2.45. The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) officiated. The mourner 4 included Colonel and Mrs. Marson (son and daughter-indaw), the deceased lady's niece, the nurse who had attended her, Mr. Henry Greenall, Mr. John White and Mr. Charles White. The whole of the arrangements were carried out by Garnett's, Warrington. Skating Carnival. 'The skating rink in Artingstali's Buildings pre- sented a pretty and animated appearance on Thursday evening when the first skatinecaraival was in process. Picturesque and humorous costumes were greatly in evidence. Diff-rent nationalities were strikingly represented and a great feature of the evening was the originality of the dress3s. Thera were such novel impersonations as Carrie Naticn (the well known saloon smasher), "The lilickwatch " and a footballer who had lately been in the wars and was consequently swathed in bandages. Spanish mutileers were also splendidly portrayed and last but not least was "The Territorial." The prize for fancy skaking was secured by Miss Shearer, and the awards for most humorcus costumes -were :—Gentlemen, Mr. G. Bowcock (dressed as Carrie Nation) ; ladies, Mrs. A. Walker (as an Indian Squaw). All three prize winners are local patrons ol the rink: The carnival was very successful and it is hoped to hold a second one in the near future.
