Death of Mr. William Lawless. • Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death of Mr, William Lawless, who passed away at his residence, 25, Arpley-street, on Siturday afternoon. The deceased gentleman, who was in his 81st year, had been confined to the house for about eight weeks, the cause of death being senile decay. For tile remarkable period of neatly 70 years he was with the firm of Messrs. Dakin and Banks, cheese factors, Horsemarket street, having entered their service when quite a boy. When Messrs. Dakin and Banks gave up the business, Mr. Lawless to )1c charge of it until the stata of his health compelled him to remain at home. Mr. Lawless was a Conservative in politics and a member of the Church of England. He was closely attached to St. Paul's Church, and had held the office of sidesmen. The funeral took pli)ce at the Cometery on Tuesday afternoon, the Rev. H. V. Pigot officiating. The principal mourners were Mr. Joseph Lawless (son), Mr. George Dakin, Mrs. W. IL Lawless (Sankey), Mr. and Mrs. Benbrook (Liverpool), Mr. G. Smith, Mr. George H Smith, Mr Peter Simkins, Mr Newns, Mr. Leigh (Tarvin), Mr. Hesketh and Mr. Briggs (Arpley-street). div.head: IRELAND'S NATIONAL
div.p: IRELAND'S NATIONAL
FESTIVAL.
By Austin M. Crowe.

Another Et. Patricks' Day has cane and gene, an 1 909 has found Irishmen still possessing that wonder ful devotion to the name of their illustrious Patron Saint. It is an undisputed fact that the Irish National Festival is more universally celebrated than that of it any other nation, and a few reflections_ on it are certainly seasonable. The Irish race are the most widely spead nation on the face of the earth, even the Jew being left behind. In this country there is a large Irish population, and all over the continent one may find their descendants. In Spain, in Austria, in France, some of the greatest and noblest families are of direct Irish'descent. Perhaps the broken treaty of Limerick can be attributed as the principal cause for this, as many Irish soldiers of rank and name carried their swords abroad after this unhappy event. To Australia thousands of Irishmen and Irishwomea have for years annually emigrated, so that now Erin's sons are pitnninent in Church, in Commerce, and in State. South Africa, too, has her quota, whilst South America and Canada have each an influential and substantial Irish population. it is, however, in the great Republic of the West where the Irish exile has indelibly made his mark. In that vast territory the. Irish and the Irish-American are counted by millions and enormous is their influence. They are to be met in every walk of life; they are--in the ranks of the highest, and amongst the poorest. In that con- glomeration of races which goes to make up the United States, Irishmen have played a great and responsible part. It is left to the present President of the land of Stars and Stripes, Mr. Taft, to sum up the Irish character, who in a speech delivered in New York on St. Patrick's Day' 1908, made use of the following remarks. He saki- " Their fidelity to their religious faith, their stubborn resistance to the enforcement of laws which separated them from the soil they owned, their brilliant valour on every battlefield, their gallantry, their delightful sense_ of humour, their poetic fervour and tempera- ment, and the quickness with which the tear follows the smile, continue unabated in the Irish strain, whether you find it in the land of their origin,or in the many distant lands whence its enterprise and energy may have carried representatives of the race." One could write chapters and chapters and yet not deal adequately with the achievements of the Irish exile. The names of Emund Burke, Dean Swift, Sheridan, Goldsmith and Sterne stand out in English history amongst the greatest of her statesmen, philosophers and writers. In Military affairs it is only necessary to speak of the Duke of Wellington, Lords Wolseley, Roberts, and Kitchener', whilst .at the Bar, Hugh Cairns and Lord Russell of Killowen, are sufficient proof of their qualities of justice. Of Parliamentary orators the names. of Flood and aTathan, Burke and O'Connell are a host in themselves, whilst at the present day Mr. John E. Redmond, M.P., is unani- niously voted the Orator of the House of Commons. Travelling further afield, we find prominent and loyal to the country of their adoption the Maaahons of France, the O'Donnells of Spain, and the Taaffes of Austria—a few only of the Many illustrious Irish houses. To attempt to chronicle the sons of the Emerald Isle who have won fame in America would be a heavy task. Their names crowd the / pages of history from the first governor of New York, George Clinton to the present date. The great Washington himself knew their value as was witnessed in the person of Colonel Richard Fitzgerald his aide-de-camp and bodyguard. Among his Irish generals were William Thompson, Anthony Wayne, Richard Montgomery, Andrew Lewis, Walter • Stewart, Charles Stewart, Henry Knox and John Sullivan. So also in the American Civil War their prominence was again unmistakeable. One might go on for ever, but the great fact that stares us in the face is that of the unbounded influence of the Irish race, so that we see at different and distant parts of the earth -other Irelands, big Irelands; where the 17th of March is celebrated just as enthusiastically as in the little island which they love to call their birthright. Truly indeed has St. Patrick left a great impression, and perhaps the secret of it is the manner in which he Christianised that then Pagan race. He mastered their language, their customs, their idiosyncrasies, and then by degrees he preached to and converted the whole nation to the Christian religion. It was a bloodless victory, and stands out luminously in the history of the Church as one of the greatest triumphs of Christianity. The Irish race have thus reason to be proud of their Patron, a man of saintliness and ability. Moreover, they are quite as proud of that wonderful fidelity to his memory, to their country and to its faith. There is something inexpressively grand about this love of Ireland, and whilst! such exists there is always a longing in the hearts of its sons to see their own little island again governed-by Irishmen according to Irish ideas and Irish aspirations.

div.head: Daylight Saving Bill.
div.p: The Daylight Saving Bill.
TO THE EDITOR of' THE EXAMINER.

Sir,—Will you permit me to draw the attention of your readers tqthe fact that whether the alteration of the clock be by 4 steps of 20 minutes each commenc- ing on the first Sunday in April, or whether it be by one step of one hour on the third Sunday in April the effect will be that we shall leave our beds and follow our daily pursuits at exactly the same distance from sunrise AS WE DID THIS MORNING.
Will any of your readers say that they were con- scious of any hardship this morning? Did the cows not yield milk, or did milkman overweighted with _ _ _ _

the burden of his hard lot fail to deliver the milk in time for breakfast, or did- the servants of the household fail to respond to the early summons of their alarm clock? Now, conditions of lire in regard 0 the early part of the day would be exactly the same on the morning of the first alteration as they were this morn- ing, except that as it would be rather later in the year the weather, let us hope, will be more genial. It is impossible to carry out any reform without causing some interests to suffer, but when one can prove, as can be proved in this case, that considerable advantages will accrue to at least nine-tenths of the whole population of the country, the slight and almost ridiculous objections which are . raised to the Bill should be allowed to sink out of sight. A special committee of the House of Commons is, however, about to sit in judgment on the Bill, and everything must be done in order to enable them to arrive at the truth, I, therefore, appeal to your readers to send me a statement of any evidence they will be prepared to give either for or against the Bill. It niust not be said after this committee has reported. that any interest has not been heard.—Yours faithfully,
WILLIAM WILLETT. Sloane Square, London, S.W. March 22nd, 1909.

Mr. MITC.FIELL seconded the motion, and it was enthusiastically carried.— Mr. HIPKISS briefly repliel. The Rev. T. Miller and the Naval Scare.

At gold-street on Sunday ereaing last the Rev. T. Miller took as his subject "The evil .of mar." The preacher said it was only a deep sense of responsibility which caused him to choose the subject. It sees too late for ChrMian ministers to condemn war when the battle NV et S begun.. rhe present moment was opportune before a nasal scare had developed into a ristionat conflict; A few principles would he accepted by all classes. Our great oversga trade deman,ded a strong navy and our homes must be secured. All wars were net evil. Some struggles, o g., . the war between North and South America, were for the extension of liberty.. Our powerful Navy made the abolitien of the slave trade porsinle. So few Wars were, however, justified by history, that a man Would not he very-insane who accepted the principle," l'eace at any price." In the immediate future we must guard against panic. We musL recognise that our neighbours. ha 4- the right of expansion ; also that their commerce required protection. If we would he believed we must also believe their protestations of fi iendliness. National labels were not- of Divine inspiration. We must recognise our kinship with the German race. Theologically we owed to that country an incalculable debt of gratitude. It was the home of the Reformation; the birth-place of Biblical criticism. Considering the importance of the issues, the unwise speech of Mr. Bonar-Law ought to mean the ruin of his political career. War was a great physical evil. :Its methods vtere barbarous. Suffering was inflicted upon

men who before had lived ignorant of each other's existence. We were told it made heroes; it also made widows and orphans. Its great evil was that the suffering was caused by men. Monolly it was disastrous. The finer sentiments were almost lost in a time of conflict. The fiercest passions were liberated. Again it placed in the ascendancy a class—the military—which hal little regard for liberty. 'There were fine Christian soldiers but the influence tf a class must not be judged by its excepti.ns. Militarism must not be judged by General Gordon or the Lawrances and Havelocks. All social reform was arrested when. war began. If ever the country was to meet the needs of its aged poor, its invalid, and the great problems of poverty be solved, a peaceful policy was absolutely necessary. It was impossible to avoid the suspicion that fear of social reform bad been the inspiration of the present scare. Amongst the causes of war Were mentioned an untrue conception of patriotism. It was not necessary to consider our country always right. An-other cause was a fear of criticising the Govern- ment. Statesmen were often blinded by party politics. We slid into war. We must advocate* arbitration. During the past six years six first class questions which would have led to war had teen sett7ed by,arbitration. It was thecaltnness of Lord Salisbut y,when the American President had lost his disc!et ion,that saved us from war, by submitting the Venezuelan questions to arbitration. We- had a treaty with France by which almost all possible causes of war between us were to be submitted to arbitration. It was only moneyed interests which prevented a similar treaty being ratisfied between this country and America. Why could not a similar treaty he established between Germany arid ourselves? Every Christian must realize the responsibility of citizenship and exert his influence on the side of peirte and pro- gress. The time would come when the instruments of war would be the implements of peaceful industry.

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.

CAPTAIN CROSFIELD'S MILITARY TRAINING GILL. An Attack on the Government.

From educational differences, the members of our local Parliament turned their attention on Tuesday evening to military topics. Captain G. R. Crosfield, the Independent member . for Rochdale, introduced a Bill " to make compulsory the military training of the youth of Great Britain " and the ensuing discussion had already given rise to considerable interest and excitement when the House adjourned until Tuesday evening next. Captain CROSFIELD, who was loudly applauded. from all quarters of the House on r:sing to support his pro- posals, confessed that he belonged to that tribe which Lord Morley Old us we were to avoid at all costs—the man who sat en tho hedge, looked down en either side, and feared to take the plunge because he thought the ditch was too deep. (Laughter.) But althouah he might be a wobbler in party politics-s-(laughter)—and that was why be stood there as a non-party 'man. th i. was one subject over which he had never wobbled since he took it up, and over which le never intended to wobble, and that was the question of com- pulsory military training. (Applause). The only party he could Dot, get a quotation from was the Nationalist party, but as they ((ese always fighting amongst themselves it might be said that they were a nation in arms already. (Laughter.) If we were going to be -Made to surrender it would only be by an ermy landed on these shores—only by being defeated in battle. It was to preecnt that that we required our young men to be trained, that we required our hacks 1 and our goal-keeper to be trained before the mActi beean and not afterwards. " I say," declared the Captain, " that vie are in a most critical position, tbat this country will be in very serious danger in the years to come, andi am perfectly prepared to prove that." div.head: CROYDON BY-ELECTION.
div.p: THE CROYDON BY-ELECTION.

To many men there is no sport so good as that which a parliamentary election may be made to provide, and the people of Croydon have not been slow to make the most of the Opportunity wbich focusses the -attention of the country upon their choice. Sir Robert Hermon-Hodge, the Unionist candidate, is an old parliamentary hand. He has gone through eight elections as candidate, and has been three times elected. He sat for South Oxfordshire during the years from 1895 to 1906, and previously he was Member for six Years for the North-Eastern Division of Lancashire. His Liberal opponent, Mr. J. E. Raphael, has hitherto been content to shine as a m Dst brilliant athlete, and he has found it rather hard to be taken seriously in any other sphere. He is a barrister with great ambition, and the House of Commons generally invites men of his character sooner or later.

The warm discussion as to the British and German naval policies has drawn much attention to the Secretary of State fcr the Navy, Admiral von Tirpitz, who denied the statements made in the House of Commons, and declared that in 1912 his country would have and not 17 battleships of the Dreadnought type. He also denied that any proposal or disarmament had been made by England to Germany. Some uncertainty prevails as to the exact facts upon which his statement was based. In some quarters it is contended that he has left the armoured cruisers of the Invincible type which Germany is constructing out of his calculations, while the Premier and Mr. Balfour included them in their estimate of both British and German strength. The Admiral declares that the sole aim of the German naval Programme is to preserve peace. .

div.head: PICTURES OF THE WEEK.
div.p: PICTURES OF THE WEEK.
Fire in Bridge-street.

A fire which resulted in the destruction of the building and a loss of over .£l,OOO, broke out between the hours of one and two on Tuesday morning in the workshop of , Messrs. Huggett and Worthington Ltd., electricians &c., S 5, Bridge-street. A policeman was making his usual round of examining theshops at about fen minutes past one when he discovered that the door of the storeroom belonging to Messrs. Huggett and Worthington Was not locked. Mr. Huggett was aroused and came down. He then locked the door and went to bed again. A few minutes afterwards he was informed that the works, in which were stored finished and unfinished cycles, and machinery, and in which electro-plating and stove-enamelling &c., is done, was on. fire. 'The place was destroyed in a very short time. How the fire originated is a mystery. Soon after the outbreak the Superintendent of the Fire Brigade, ,the Deputy superintendent and several men were quickly on the scene with the engine Captain, and they are to be complimented upon preventing the flames spreading to adjoining buildings.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS.
ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH.

St. John's Presbyterian Church, after a full century' of religious usefulness, is passing to secular uses, and the time seems appropriate for a brief account of its early history. A hundred years ago "St. John's" was the centre to which an earnest and numerous body of Nonconformists gathered. Their minister, Alexander Hay, was in the zenith of his powers and was attracting a congre- gation of influential men and women whose names stood high in the roll of local worthies. The congregation had an interesting origin.

div.head: GLAZEBROOK CLASS MEETINGS.
div.p: GLAZEBROOK CLASS MEETINGS.

In 1777 St. James' Church, Latchford was built and its first incumbent was James Glazebrook. An earnest &angelical he toiled hard for twenty years, and drew to his side a large and like-minded congrega- tion. His work was shared by John Harmer, a former helper of John Wesley, who preached at the openinc, of the church and whose zeal was scarcely less than that of the vicar. Mr. Glazebrook himself had studied at the Countess of Huntingdon's College at Trevecca and was ever a man of broad and wide-reaching sympathies. Like many Puritan ministers he' encouraged the forma- tion of a society within, his church which met separately from it and for the purpose of holding purely spiritual worship. These meetings were held often in the homes of the members and were conducted as Methodist or Quaker meetings might be. To those who assembled, the zealous minister gave of his best and at the period of his death in 1803 the society had become a centre of great influence. SEPARATION FROM ST. JAMES'.

The incumbent next appointed had no syn-rpathy towards the irregular meetings of the congregation and took up an attitude of opposition. Cleavage was inevitable. Unable to worship in comfort at St. James' the society decided to withdraw from the Establishment and seek a home elsewhere. For public worship they united with the Congregationalists who met in Stepney ChaOel, though without entering into membership with them. They preserved their entity by continuing to meet on week evenings in each other's homes. It could hardly be expected that this arrangement would last. Trained in the Church of England they were attached to the service ana Sacraments, and desired to retain a form of service which was endeared to them by many associations. Unable to adapt them- selves to Congregational methods, and unwilling to yield their liberty, after three years they decided to begin to meet as a separate religious body. A large room which had served successively for Methodist and Roman Catholic worship was rented and services conducted with Anglican ritual began to be held in the early months of 1806. Correspondence was entered into with Dr. Ford of London, the result of which was the settlement of Alexander Hay as their minister. In July 1806 his first_ sermon was preached and he began a ministry which lasted with growing power and influence for nearly twenty-one years. The room soon became too small for the numbers who came to hear him, and in the summer of 1807 the erection of St. John's Church was begun. The lease bears date May 30th, 1807. Our only knowledge of the leaders of the Church is such as can be gleaned from the names in the lease and baptismal register. The Register dates from 1806, and opens with the name of Elizabeth Heath baptized lon April 4th in that year. Names of frequent loccurrence are Thomas Haddock, builder, John Edleston, pin maker; Peter 'Lever, muslin manufacturer; John Long, Thomas Bocock, butcher, of Cock Hill, and Banks, Letherbrow, Dakin and Hodgkinson—good old Warrington names—are often repeated.

div.head: "HAY'S CHAPEL."
div.p: "HAY'S CHAPEL."

The building began its era of usefulness in January 1808. Its eloquent and zealous minister was the preacher and the crowded congregations which flocked to listen to him gave promise of a great future. For almost twenty years his ministry at St. John's.was a strong factor in the life of the town. Earnest and fearless, he never lacked a con- gregation. Popular with the poor he drew also the rich, as the long row of Sunday morning carriages told. So completely did the congregation centre in the minister that for eighteen years there does not appear to have been any attempt to prepare a trust deed, and if any church was organized we do not know upon what basis. St. John's was "Hay's Chapel" for every practical purpose, though technically it appears to have been regarded as belonging to the Countess of Huntingdon Connexion. The death of Alexander Hay occurred on May 17th, 1827, and he was buried at the foot of his pulpit, the scene of the great labour and triumph of his life. During the three years which followed his death rapid changes took place. Various ministers ocqupied the pulpit, among whom were James Durant,Sampson Hawtkorne,Ebenezer Morley, George Smith and Dr. James Stewart.
In 1830 the Chapel, passed into hands of the Seotch Secession Church. The Church would. therefore become Piesbyterian but no record of the period has been pre- served.

div.head: FURTHER CHANGES.
div.p: FURTHER CHANGES.

After five years the congregation again joined itself to the Countess of Huntingdon Connexion, and in 1836 called Rev. Caleb Bird as its minister. The church continued until 1851, when by its own resolution it was disbanded and re-formed upon a new basis. A new minister, Rev. E. J. Hartland, had been called and began a useful ministry, but differences arose with the officials of the Lady Huntingdon Connexion and the church decided to secede. Salem Chapel, the present Golborne-street Baptist Church,was in disuse and the congregation migrated thither in November 1852. Two years later the church was admitted into the Congregational Union, but in 1855 decided to become a Baptist meeting with open Communion. After two years of disuse St. John's became the home of a Presbyterian Church. Purchased by Mr. Barbour of Manchester, it was given to the congregation. The iministers since that period have been Revs. IJames Wood 1854-59, Andrew Inglis 1859-61, IJ. B. Johnson 1863-76, James Warnock • 1877-1900, J. L. Milne 1902-1909. The history of the Church during the past generation is sufficiently known to our readers. Presbyterianism is not indigenous to England and labours at some natural dis- advantage. In the case of St. John's many things have made the struggle a hard one, and the fabric has been sold in the hope that a re-establishment of the church in more congenial surroundings may be possible. Many will regret that we are to have one church the less,for the neighbourhood stands in need of it, more greatly perhaps than when the saintly Alexander Hay began his work a 6entury ago.

OUR MISCELLANY.

We are glad to know that our brief sketch of the history of Roman Catholic worship in Warrington has been welcomed as a valuable contribution to a subject over which a haze has long been resting. Several facts remain to be added and in chronicling these we shall leave the narrative as complete as the available record and traditions allow. By the kindness of Father Whittle we are able to use some traditional matter taken from the lips of the late Father Bury. ** * *

The first meeting place to which Warring- ton Catholics are said to have gathered was a moated G-range about three miles south of Hindley. Here in the time of Charles I. Mass was celebrated with more or less secrecy and there were those who walked over to attend. Father Bury was priest-in- charge at Hindley and told how he had visited the old Grange and seen traces of its moat and ancient portcullis. The priest's hiding hole still existed and over the entrance of the room used as a chapel was the repre- sentation of a chalice. The building com- pleted its careqr of usefulness as a barn and after some years collapsed owing to sub- sidence of the land from colliery workings.

It is suggested that worship was secretly established about the year 1700 but no definite date can be given. An interesting description of the old room behind the Feathers Inn appears to have been given to Father Bury by some one. The room was ostensibly a sack warehouse. It was approached by a small dark passage pur- posely arranged on a tortuous plan and at each angle in an approach a watcher is said to have been placed. The sack room itself formed the upper floor. A trap door in the centrd would allow anyone to drop down to the floor below. A heap of old sack covered this secret exit, and in the event of an alarm from the watchers the priest and emblems passed • rapidly from sight. Sacks were thrown over the door and the worshippers busied themselves in mending them. Such mending must have proved a useful foil for we are told that when another room became the place of meeting the sack and bag business was the ostensible purpose for which it was hired.-

The early services would be conducted by visiting priests but their names have not been preserved. The earliest name associated with the ministry is that of Father Bennet Shuttleworth, who had long been at Woolston, and'who in 1771 received permis- sion to visit Warrington and establish a Mission. He only lived until 1774. Four Years later by the efforts of Father Bradshaw the Mission was placed upon a firm basis by the building of the first Chapel in Bewsey- street.

An interesting relic of the first resident priest is preserved at St. Alban's Church in the form of a door jbandle brought by him from Lamspring. It bears the form of a lamb and is attached to one of the doors of the Church. The pictures carried by him from the same place are in tile possession of Mr. Peter Caldwell. -

Few of our old buildings have come to a more fitting use than the Old Fox Inn in Buttermarket-street. No happier purpose could have been chosen for it than that it should have become a miniature museum of antiquities. Among recent relics which have come into the hands of Mr. Robert Lewis, its proprietor, is a fine sample of a loving cup which for several generations belonged to the family of Thomas Eaton .of Stockton Heath.

The Eaton family has a history worth recording. One of,the earlier members of it was Rector of Great Budworth and gave up the living rather than subscribe to the Act of Uniformity in 1662. Thomas Eaton became local manager of the Bridgwater Canal at the wish of the Duke of Bridgwater and lived in the house now occupied by Dr. Willett. He is remembered as a friend of the early Methodists, his name appearing in their journals with many grateful comments. To him and to the late William Clarke our district owes the distinction which it has gained as the birthplace of the Total Abstinence Movement for it was by his interest and endeavour that the first society was formed some eighty years ago.

div.head: BLACKBURN PHILANTHROPIC BURIAL SOCIETY.
div.p: BLACKBURN PHILANTHROPIC BURIAL SOCIETY.

Notwithstanding trade depression, the Blackburn Philanthropic Burial Society has had a very successful year, as the summary of the annual report, published in our advertising columns, indicates. The society is one of the most remarkable societies transacting industrial insurance. Established in 1839, it has thus had seventy years' experience of the business. Its benefits are among the most liberal of any eociety in the country. For example, a premium of Id. per week at age 11 next birthday, purchases a policy of £l2 10s., payable at death. This, it is claimed, is a far greater amount than is allowed by any other industrial company or society in the country. This remark also applies to practically the whole of the society's tables. But the society is not weakened in any way by giving these( extremely liberal benefits. The reason why it is able to give such good terms is, firstly that it is economiCally managed, the proportion of the premiums spent in commission and expenses teing much less than by most of the industrial companies and societies. Secondly there are no shareholders to absokb any of the profits, which belong exclusively to the members. At the end of 1905, for instance, the assets exceeded the liabilities, valued on a stringent basis, by no- less than £135,299. The members, there- fore, receive the benefit of these profits in the shape of increased assurances, and this is the reason why the Society gives much better value than the average com- pany or society. The funds at December 31st, 1908, stood at £479,203 4s. 31r1„ having been increased during the year by the unprecendented amount of £36,132. Ten yews ago the funds amounted to £215,909. "Trade depression"states the report "affected a large ma jorit y of our members, and one result was that many who have never done so before were compelled to allow their con- tributions to fall into arrear,and some,unfortunately,bave suffered to such an axtent that they have had to lapse their assurances. In hot Ii cases your Board have extended their sympathy and granted concessions as each individual case has merited, and, as a result, a great proportion of such business has been retained, or re- entries have been made on equitable terms. The trade depression had another effect, and that was the non. .realisation of the ambition of your Board of Maniige- ment, namely, a Premium Income for 1908 of £lOO,OOO. However, an increase of, it is submitted, a very gratify- ing amount, was obtained, the said Income being increased by a sum of £5,703, making an income from premiums alone of £97,001 ; within easy reach of the desired amount. The premium income for 1897 was £54,385 9s. 10d. The total income amounts to £113,493 compared with £106.253 for 1907, en increase of £7,240. A work of consolidation of the business has been going on dnring the past year. Those districts opened up just previous thereto are doing well, and, to assist further in giving confidence to members and the public generally, offices have recently been taken in Ardwick-green, Manchester; Chorley, Blackpool and Southport. Further, the claim- rate, your Board is pleased to report, is 1.46 per cent. .of the .premium income less than the experience of 1907—a very important feature—although the number of claims paid, namely, 4,876, and amount £42,785 Os. 5d., are greater than those of 1907 by 13 In number and by £1,187 17s. 81d. in amount. This sum makes the claims paid during the last 13 years into £429,756." All further information esti be obtained from the Warrington District Office, Carlton House Chambers, Sankey-street. Mr. Joseph Frirhurst is the superin- tendent.

div.head: BURST MAINS CAUSE A WATER FAMINE.
div.p: BURST MAINS CAUSE A WATER FAMINE.

The bursting of two water-mains at Coatbridge on Monday morning deprived a district of five square miles of water. The accident occurred in the main street, which was undermined for a distance of 200 yards, the causeway being raised several inches, and the tramway track was washed away in places.
S MY LIFE STOR

div.head: ALDERMAN LUKE ELLIsON, J.P.
div.p: ALDERMAN LUKE ELLIsON, J.P.

Quiet arid uneventful though my life has been, it has witnessed such great changes and developments in Warrington and par- ticularly in the Latchford district, with which I have been so long associated, that possibly my recollections may be of some little interest to your readers.. I was born at Martinscroft, near Warrington, on March 18th, 1836. My father Thomas Ellison was a hand-looni weaver up to his twenty-fifth year, but with the advent Of machinery his old occupation disappeared,and he had to turn his attention .to labouring. He removed to. Latchford two years after I was born and was employed on the Old Warps farm, now Victoria Park, for over twenty years. There was an old dame school at what is now called Brook Place, kept by a Mrs. Carter, a widow, and in my childhood days I used to go there and try to read a chapter in the Bible and receive a little instruction. That was prac- tically all the " schooling" I received, except at Sunday school. For about eighteen years I attended the Primitive Methodist Sunday school in Old-road, and I remember during that time taking part in the procession which "walked the boundary" on the incorporation of the Borough. At about ten years of age I worked in the fields alone with my father. A year later I was apprenticed to the shoe trade with Mr. Bostock, who had a shop in Bridge-street next door to where Mr. Wm. Roberts' premises now stand. After serving there for two years I was transferred to Mr. Newall's, The Ackers, Latchford, where I completed my apprentice- ship and also worked a further two years as a journeyman before commencing business on my own account in Knutsford-road, not far from my present premises.

Latchford, as I picture it in those early days, was an old-fashioned country village. Looking from the corner of Thelwall-lane one saw an expanse of common land, with a few thatched cottages and farm houses scattered here and there. Grappenhall- road, Thelwall-road, Knutsford-road and Wash-land had open ditches on each side, and the cartways were paved with cobbles. I have seen the erection of !practically the whOle of the Latchford of to-day. When I was a boy it used to be a matter of dread almost to go from Warrington to Latchford at night; it was such a wild region. MerAey View has been built in my time. Warrington, too, has undergone a great transformation within my recollection. The shops in Bridge- street used to be approached by three or four steps and had bay windows. Watchmen patrolled the streets during the night, trying doors and shutters, and at certain points they had to call out the hour and whether it was a fine night or not. The Warrington Police Force as an organization had not come into being; there were just one or two constables. Warrington was served by one railway and Bank Quay Station after the style of Latchford Station. I was eleven years of age when I first saw a train. The Old Warps was part of Thelwall at that time but the lodge, which stood on an island, was considered to be in Warrington. The river wound round almost to the Manor Locks and there were some terrible floods,the meadow land through Thelwall and even as far as Lymm being practically one mass of water. I also recollect an extraordinary hailstorm that occurred when I was seventeen years of age. It was on the 24th June. The hailstones were of such remarkable size-4; inches round—that windows were broken, vegetation seriously damaged, and fowls ran screaming to shelter. As showing the advantages which the present generation enjoy, it may be worth mentioning that my father used to make his own matches. He dipped thin pieces of wood into brimstone and ignited them by means of a tinder and flint.

One of my chief hobbie§ on entering into business in Latchford was music, and I took part in the formation of the Latchford Brass band. Twelve months after our formation the first company of local Vplunteers was started at Manor House, Latchford, and they persuaded our band to join in a body and play for them. We did so for six years and during that_time four or five companies were formed and Captain Greenall became the colonel. When we retired Mr. Oakden,our bandmaster, induced me and several other members to join the 4th S. Lancashire Militia Band, which was then stationed at Warrington. I served in that band for five years, under the command of the late Colonel Blackburne. The instrument I played in those days was the bombardon. On leaving the band I was appointed the first sub-postmaster of Latch- ford, and held the position for twenty-seven years. At an early age I became identified with the Primitive Methodist denomination but when the Wesleyans formed a society in Latchford I threw in my lot with them. In the meantime I had some small share in the building of Christ Church, Latchford, and I had the pleasure of helping the late Rev. Richard G-reenall in the work there for a short time. The Good Templary movement has always been dear to my heart. In 1873 I was instrumental in forming the Bonehill Lodge at Latchford. We first held our meet- ings in an old barn on the site of the present Wesleyan Church. There was a Wesley Lodge in Warrington and the members came to pay us a visit, the outcome being that the room was secured for Wesleyan services and Sunday School work, as well as for Good Templary meetings. Ultimately we removed to the Temperance Hall where we continued Ithe work for sixteen years, and the present commodious Wesleyan Church was then built. I was twenty-six years of age when I joined the Wesleyan Methodists and I am proud to say I have continued with them down to the present day. I have been honoured by election to all- the lay offices, including those of Sunday school superin- tendent, chapel steward, treasurer and trustee. Two years ago I relinquished Sunday school work, feeling that advancing years and long service demanded that I should take a rest. Nothing has afforded me greater satisfaction than to see the progress of the Wesleyan Church in this neighbour- hood. We have now a large and well- appointed Sunday school and the opening' of

the new organ in the church last week was perhaps the crowning achievement. From my youth I have taken an interest in municipal work and in 1895 I acceded to the request that I should contest Latchford Ward in the Liberal interest. I was returned after a contest with Mr. Lin. Greening and had the honour of re-election on three occasions, though I was opposed each time Twelve months ago, as your readers are well aware, I was elevated to an aldermanic seat. Political affairs have always possessed a great interest for me and I have known the day when the fact of being a Liberal caused one to be regarded with a certain amount of opprobrium. In the long run, however, I believe I have lost nothing by adhering to the progressive views which I conscienti- ously hold. I have a lively recollection of the old " nomination " days when the candidates appeared on the hustings which used to be erected on the old fair ground near Messrs. Peter Walker's Brewery in King-street. There was no lack of excitement then ! I can just remember the keen contest between the late Mr.— afterwards Sir—Gilbert Greenall and Mr. William Allcard in 1847, when Mr. Greenall was returned by a majority of 29. From that year up to 1868 Mr. Greenall repre- sented Warrington unopposed. In 1867 Parliament had passed the Reform Act which gave the franchise to workingmen, and naturally the greatest interest was taken in the first local election under the new conditions. Mr. Peter Rylands was prevailed upon to undertake the apparently hopeless task of contesting the borough against Mr. Greenall, and no effort was spared by the Liberals to ensure his return. On the day of the election excitement was at fever heat, and at the close of the poll it- was announced that Mr. Greenall had been returned by a majority of 78. Great was the rejoicing of the Conservatives, but when a scrutiny was made Mr. Rylands was declared elected by a majority of 27. It may interest your readers to know that my father's brother, Luke Ellison, was one of the first to be employed at the Crewe railway works. When he first went there only about a dqzen workmen were engaged, and everyone knows to what an enormous extent the works have grown. He was a great Primitive Methodist, and lived to be eighty-six years of age. At the funeral,. which I attended, the procession was nearly a mile long. My father almost attained his eightieth year—in fact, our family has a reputation for longevity. _

In 1859 I married Ann Clare, of Houghton Green, Middleton, and last month we, received very gratifying congratula- tions on our golden wedding. We have two sons and two daughters living and, like ourselves, they are life-long teetotallers and have also married abstainers. Our eldest son, the Rev. Joseph Ellison, became a Baptist and entered the ministry. He went out to America to marry the girl of his early choice, Anne, daughter of Henry Whitham, who some years ago emigrated to America. Returning to this country, he was chosen for the pastorate • of Zion Baptist Church, Ynysybwl, which he at present holds. Our other son, David, is a stationmaster at Preston.

div.head: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON. A Word to the Children.
div.p: BEAUTIFUL WARRINGTON. A Word to the Children.

My dear Beautiful Warrington Children, Have we not had a long cold winter? Here we are at the end of March, whose winds should "stir the dancing daffodil" and yet I have not even the bud of a daffodil showing in my garden. How bare and desolate it still looks--only a few crocuses and aconites trying to beautify the dull brown earth But, I know that. while it has been dreary outside, you have had colour and sweetness in the home. The lovely flowers exhibited at the bulb show, whispered to .me of the loving care which you had bestowed upon your bulbs and how in return they had beautified your home, while tte gardens and fields were sad and dreary. Children, eo you know I see some gardens sad even in the summer hen, because they have put on their brightly coloured dresses, they should be gay and smiling. Roor gardens! I want the mem- bers of our Society to help to dress them this summer. They are like little children; they need assistance from others in putting on their clothes. Latchford is a poor entrsnre to this old town; but, if the householders would only spend a little energy and a few pence, it would te vastly improved. Many of the houses possess a little garden at the front, which is really no garden, for these door patches of Mother earth, are as hard and bare as the roadway. Will the children who live in Latchford persuade the owners to cultivate these little- gardens ? In fact, wherever you see a garden neglected, USA your influence to make it a thing of beauty. The other day I saw a bill on a wall headed "Protec- tion of Birds." How sad it is to think that laws have to be mado to protect our little songsters. There is something of the savage in those people who wantonly destroy them. During the bitter snowy weather which we had just after Christmas, I saw bunches of pretty feathered birds being sold in the market at 3d. a dozen. I felt sorry as I thought how these little songsters had come to man for food during those frosty days, and how they had been cruelly put to death. Their songs would have made the woods merry this summer and•now they are bushed for ever. This incident made me think of a little story 1. once read:—" A pleasant little village was surrounded by orchards. The trees were a beautiful sight in the spring; and on the branches, and in the hedges, the birds sang their sweetest. And in the autumn, apples and pears and plums could be seen everywhere. One spring, some wicked boys made up their minds to destroy every nest they could find. The poor birds, frightened by this strange act flew away from the village, and not a single note could be heard. All around seemed sad and silent. Now that their enemies, the birds, were gone the destructive worms could do as they liked, and they soon stripped the trees of lelf and blossom. The orchards were as bare as in winter, and the wicked boys who had always been able to have plenty of fruit, could not get a single apple to eat." Children, do not be tempted to take the nests or to destroy our little feathered friends, for they do more- good than harat—Yours affectionately,
V.M.T.

div.head: SYNOPSIS.
div.p: SYNOPSIS.

HENRY HASTONARD, a student of sculpture in Paris, has peen left a fortune of seven thousand pounds a year on condition that he is earning five hundred pounds a year by his own labour and talent by the time he is twenty-five. If that condition is unfulfilled the money is to go to a cousin. Gastonard is now twenty-four, and there seems to be no prospect of his ever receiving the fortune. He writes to his friend Paddy O'Connell telling of his acquaintance with Mimi—" The Show Girl"—and an ad- venture with a gang of Apaches, who attack him in Paris„ having designs upon a gold and diamond cigarette-case which they think he carries, but which is actually in Idimfs possession. To the opportune arrival of the police Henry is indebted for escaping from the ruffians with a whole skin, but he Mils himself with Mimi on his hands, for the girl, who has restored to Harry the cigarette case, dares not return to her former associates. She tells him all she knows of her history, which is not much. She remembers, far back in her childhood, an old lady who WM kind to her, and after that, she has no knowledge of any other life but that of a show-girl, travelling about the country with a lion-tamer, of whom she still stands in terror. At his *it's end to know what to do with his protege, Gastonard appeals to his friend Madame Lea d'Alencon.

Gastonard is convinced tle:t Mimi has dramatic talent, and it is decided that she shall study for a year to lit her- self for the stage. Captain d'Alencon, husband of Madame Lea, is of opinion—quite mistakenly—that he has a cause of quarrel against Gastonard. in 1 challenges him to a duel. A letter to friend Paddy O'Connell brings the Irishman post haste to Paris, and he arrives to fi:al Henry wounded and being nursed by Mimi.
CHAPTEP, IX.
[Being a further instalment of the Story from the pen of Paddy O'Connell.]
Hotel St. Paul. Paris. June 30th, 1905.

Dear Clara,—l address this to you from the Hotel St. Paul; but I would have vou to know that I am theSe two days at Poissy, which is a riverside hamlet at the gates of Paris. Harry. is here with me, looking all his old self, and the little witch of a Greuze girl. We fish all daytand catch nothing. and at night we 'listen to the singing when there is any. • But, .oh, my dear Clara, 'tis the oddes,t folk in the world which comes to this place, and no people for the back drawing. room at ill. But that is between you and me, and need not be told to our neighbours at Glendalough. Ye should know that the Seine winds about Paris, and is here a pretty river enough, with a bit of a feathery island and an inn, to which the Bohemians come when they are not playing at the theatres. such a company they are The prettiest women of Paris, dressed in collars and straw hats (and not always so much as that upon them), and the drollest figures of men that I ever clapped eyes upon. They spend the morn- ings upon the river bank or in their barges, fishing for gudgeons which they do not catch ; but in the afternoons they go off to make love in the woods, and come back as brazen as the colleens from a fair. In the evenings we have dinner and music ; and pretty enough it is to sit out in the moon- light and listen to these merry nightingales when%they are in the mood to amuse us. This is the outside of the platter, .Clara; but the inside is not so vleasing by a long way. For one thing, I have discovered that the litle simpleton Mimi i 4 head over ears in love with my friend Harry, and he is not far short of that with her. And if this was not the worst of it, what should: happen but that he had a visit last night from the very last person in Paris who ought to be seen with ban, and she none other than the Captain's wife, Lea d'Alencon. _ .

Oh, 'tis a pretty business entirely, and enough to drive a sane man silly. I had be- lieved that he was done with Madame Lea for good (as he ought to be, for her folly has got him into trouble enough). The weeks that have -passed since the duel have hardly brought her name up betwixt us. I said that she was bark 'with" her. husband, who would learn .to treat- her • better; when what should happen but that she turns up at dusk last night, in a fine automobile with a nigger man driving, and is closeted a full hour with Harry to my certain knowledge. To say that I was angry is but to express my feelings -poorly. You will be my judge in that. It would have been about eight when. Lea came. ,Harry had gone up from the boat to the hotel, and I 'was helping Mimi to carry up .the tea things, for we had been for a: bit of a picnic, and a merry one, forsooth. I saw the -automobile and a veiled woman get- ting out of it ; but the child was the first to recognise Lea, and she had no pleasure of the meeting, you may be sure.
"That ,is Madame d'Alencon," says she, as pale ,as a little ghost when she said it.
- "Madame whO-r asked I, not wishing to believe it.
-Madame Lea," cried she. it be anyone else?"
"How could
"Oh, come," says I, "there's more than one Madame whoM he knows in Paris."

She stamped her foot, just like a wild beast scenting its prey. "You -know it is Madame d'Alewn, Mr. Paddy. Why do you not prevent it?" s "What Shall I bundle her into the car and send her back to Paris? Pretty talk if I did that, my dear." "She has come here to beg money of him, Mr. Paddy. You know she would not come for anything else.". "What !" cried I. in love with him?"
"Don't you think she is
. She laughed at this. long and drolly, the laugh of a woman who is shaken by a passion she _cannot express otherwise.

"Love—love--oh, what is all this talk of love? Go to her and offer money, and then come back and speak to me of love." "My dear," says I. "'tis plain- you will never be the friend of Madame Lea, in spite of what she's done for you," _ _

"Done for me, Mr. Paddy! Oh, yes, yes, yes--:she tried to prevent me seeing Monsieur Henry again. I remember that, and the English pension where I was to be locked up and treated like a school-girl, that she might be with him—her lover—while I wAs away."
"Her lover! that."
I'll not have Harry called

"It is true, true," she said, "and I--I am nailing when she is here. Why did he call himself my friend at dll? Why did he take me from the Pete? I was happy then—yes, happy, Mt. Paddy. Why did he not leave me where I wasp' _ _ _ _

She turned away from me and sobbed just for all the world like a grown woman who has come upon the supreme sorrow of her life. To be sure, Clara, I was much taken aback, and hardly knew what to say to her. Never until this moment had I understood how deeply she loved my friend, Henry Gas- tonard ; but here was all her love written down in glittering tears which a child would have understood. No longer did I doubt the story of her virtue in a society where virtue is never much more than a jest. All that had happened up at the Butte and after- yards at the Hotel St. Paul became as clear as the day. Mimi the Simpleton was ready to die for the devil-may-care English boy. I had guessed it before, but to-day I was sure of it. _ .

"Oh, come," says I, "tis hearts that are soon mended when two have the will to do it —and, see here," says I, "will,..ve be leaving him to the black woman who will ruin him, or take a hand in that affair yourself? Come up with me to the house now and hear what the lady has to say. I'll engage that neither of us will be behindhand in the civilities— and, Mimi," save I, "tis your duty to go up.,, Well, she would not hear me, but went off in a tantrum down again toward the -river and the boat. When I entered the house I discovered Harry to be closeted with Madame Lea is the little sitting-room upon the first
_ B
Y MAX. PEMBERTON
Author of "The Iron Pirate," "The
Hundred Days," "A Puritan's Wife,"
etc., etc.

flolif, and far from pleased she was to see me, 'as you will imagiue. A yozy beautiful, stately woman, as dark as the shadows upon a crimson rose and as full of passion as a caged Spaniard. I observed immediately that she had been telling the old story to my friend Harry, and with no mean success; for he paced up and down like a wild beast thinking of the country, and seemed to wel- come my intrusion as though a special provi- dence had sent me to watch over him. '
"You know Madame Lea," says he, with a wave of his hand toward her.

"If I know her," says I—and then, "I'll take leave to ask a word after Captain d'Alencon and his health." She laughed at this, saying something in French about "these droll Irishmen;" but she did not inform me that the Captain was well and, be sure, I was over-anxious about him.
"Is he in Paris Madame?" I asked her. " "rwould be good news that he was in Paris."

"Monsieur d'Alencon is at Chalons," says she, blazing up suddenly; "he has been transferred there at his own request." "Then 'tis to Chalons that you'll be going presently, Madame?" says L She did not reply to this, while Harry looked as foolish as a man can look when a woman has put a question to him and he has no mind to answer it. For my part, I was never more at my ease and I sat there watching the fair-haired lad and the grown woman, and thinking that. but for my pre- sence in that same hotel, she would carry him to Paris with her for pity's sake. "Are you fond of the fishing at Poissy, Madame?" I went on. " "fis little that they seem to catch here and a long while in the catching of IL I have taken bne gudgeon this. day, and my friend two more—tiut you will not have come here for the fishing, per- haps?"—l put it, to her. She answered me with a commonplace. Harry appeared to be greatly troubled while I spoke, and presently he could stand it no longer. "Madame d'Alencon is in trouble," he said, "I am sure you do not understand that, Paddy."

"In trouble?" pays I,- "then that's the worst news I've heard this day. Would it be about the Captain's going to Chalons?" "Captain d'Alencon has behaved like a blackguard, Paddy." "I won't doubt it. Let me meet him soon that I may tell him so."

"He has' gone to Chalons and left this poor lady almost penniless." "Then let her follow him immediately and see that someone else hears of it." "She cannot follow him, Paddy. You are talking nonsense. We must put ourselves in her position and try to help her. I'm sure that there iS not a man in Paris who would be readier to do so than my friend Paddy O'Connell." I answered this at once--

"If it's to me that she's come for advice, why here I ,am as ready with it as the best of them. For all that, her coming was an imprudence, Harry, and she'll allow me to say that she'd have done better to have stayed away."
I said this in English, for I thought that she had no knowledge of a Christian's tongue —but here I must have been mistaken, for she blazed up immediately, and said aloud that I had insulted her.

• "Who is this man?" she asked him. "Why do you permit him to say these things? Is he your friend? No; a friend would not insult your friends. I wish to speak to you alone, Harry—have I not the right to ask that?" "Certainly you have, Lea—Paddy does not mean what he says. He will understand everything better when I tell him about it °afterwards. Come, Paddy (this to me), now do be reasonable for once, and put your philo- sophy in your pocket. I am sure you are very sorry for Madame d'Alencon." "So sorry," says 1,. "that if I could meet the Captain this night, Pcl put him in the river to show the good opinion I have of him." "

They laughed together at this, and then, to change a subject which was not by way of being too delicate, Harry spoke of dinner, and the lady was quick enough to say "yes." No one in this country does much without eating or drinking ,before and after they do it; and a better ornament for a dinner-table than Lea d'Alencon you would not be finding anywhere. She is a stately, vivacious lady, living chiefly for the glory of showing herself to the gentlemen of Paris, ' and of . making love to such of them as captivate her fancy. Here, at this little inn at Poissy, she cut a fine figure enough, and sat down to the table as though • she were a queen of n mountain kingdom come down from the heights to cline with pigmies below. We sat and listened to her talk as humble ministers to an acknow- ledged wit; all of us, that is, but little Mimi the Simpleton, and she was silent enough but for one or two words of repartee that by no means discredited her.

'Twas as good as the leaping at the Horse Show; Clara, to watch the woman and the child upon opposite sides of that table, and to see the love that went flying between them.. First, it would be Madame Lea talk- ing to Harry with the grand air of the woman who finds herself in the nursery; then my little Mimi making such a grimace be- hind the lady's back that I must hold to the table with both hands to prevent the explo- sion that was within me. When Lea asks her quite affably what she . came to Poissy to ca li, Mimi answers as readily, "I came to catch myself "—and when Madame went on to say "That is a new kind of amusement" —says Mimi, "You are not too old to learn it." None the less, I knew the child was all on fire because Harry talked so much to the other one, and I was not a bit surprised when she ran away to her own room directly dinner was done, and refused to come near us for the rest of the evening. This would have been about nine o'clock; Madame left us at a quarter to eleven when Harry had told her for the twentieth time that he was not returning to Paris, and that she must go back alone. 1 saw that his re- fusal 'caused her much chagrin, but I will do him the credit to say that it was just what 1 had expected of him. When she was gone,. and we sat together for a last pipe before turning in, he asked me frankly what .were his responsibilities toward this woman, and what he ought to do for her.

"The ma; has left her, you see," says he; "he has made my friendship for her the ex- cuse, and gone off with himself to Chalons. None but a jealous Frenchman would have planned quite such a devilish revenge as that. Be doesn't divorce her, doesn't talk of a separation; but he leaves her in Paris with- out a sixpence, and then practises the mor-. alities. Confese, my dear Paddy, that there is something particularly French and subtle in all this. Lea has been accustomed to all the luxuries. She is a woman who cannot live without Wm. Poverty to her is some- thing beyond the bounds of imagination— a shadow-land too woeful to contemplate. And now d'Alencon thrusts poverty on her. He leaves her m a house of glass, whence she can see the pleasures to which she is accus- tomed, but is forbidden to take part in them. Two or three chosen servants are there to spy upon her. What alternative has such a woman if it be not an alternative of dis- honour?"

"Ye speak truly," says I, "and yet, if I were asked to name the biggest fool in Paris to-night, 'twould be this same Captain IFO.lencon. The man cannot see further 4a the end of his nose, and that, I am sure.
'e spoke between the roaring of the Lions.

iii no famous spectacle. Of course, he has no love for the woman left, and may be trying to drive her to those devices which he sus- pects, but cannot prove. Your own course is clear, Harry—you may help her if you can help her honourably. But you'll not see her again, and you'll deny yourself because you are a man of honour to begin with, and a lover in the second place:" "A lover, Paddy? What do you mean by that?"
"Just as much as I say, and not a word more. You are in love, with little Mimi up- stairs—l'd cry shame upon you if ycu were not." _ _

He was taken aback at this, and did not answer me for quite a long while. When he spoke, I knew that I had touched his heart- strings, and that he w,ould deny it no more. "If it's true, Paddy, what then?" he put it to mc. _ _ .

"Why," says I, "you'll leave for London in three days' time; get honourable employ- ment; which will save your fortune, and then come back to Paris to marry her—she, mean- while, having been at some good school to soften the manners of her." _

"Do ,you think they want softening, Paddy? " "Pm sure of it. Put all this talk of play- actresses and opera singers out of your head and come down to the truth. Mimi will make you a good wife . . . . but you'll have to teach her how."

" Shed never stop at any schocl. Paddy." "Try her and see; and, any it's done, go back to Loudon and work for your liv- ing." `` Ah," says he, rising abruptly, "it's a fine old philosopher come out of lreland after all. Well, my boy, I'll ask Mimi in the morning, and hear what ehe has to say about it." "And you'll not see the other woman again ? " "Not of my own volition, Paddy . . . upon my konour, no." "Ah, save I, "and . a fine old friend is that same volition when ye begin to weigh it up and a pretty Womh's in the balance. But I'll take what I can get," says I, " and- be thankful it's no less." - - .

Upon which, Clara; we parted; but how the promise is to be carried out, or what the future of such a man may be, God only knoWs. Now, at the very minute of closing this letter, I learn that Mimi La Godiche has left the hotel early this morning, and is no- where to be found. Such a thing was not wholly unexpected by me; but, what it may mean to my friend Harry Gastonard, I pre- fer not to think.

Never WAS a man in such a state of miiery and despair. I tan do nothing for him say nothing, think of nothing. The .child has gone, and there's an end of it. But God keep her wherever she may be is the prayer of, your affectionate brother, PADDY.

runner assurance I flat nt-, 'urea nee as nis own daughter, uttered between lengthy draughts from a capacious bottle, carried less conviction than' his story. He had, so he said, spent large sums upon her educa- tion, and taught her himself those charming accomplishments which she displayed at the many fetes her presence graced. Having in turn sold her to me (for it came to that), he asked if I thought be had no sense of honour, no finer feeling than to play the part of a mean kidnapper, taking young women from respectable homes? I This I answered immediately in the negative—for who would contradict a showman with half dozen lions at his back !

Admit, my dear Paddy, that this quest i 8 not a little pitiful, when you remember the, object of it. Consider what my acquaint- ances would say of inc if. they heard that ,my latest occupation is to search the booths about Paris for a child who wias capering with a tambourine a few months ago, and may now be returned to that employment. With these I myself should not argue. There is a day in every man's life when he must stand outside the world's conventions, break with all common tradition, and write the page of action for himself. Such a day is mine—l am indifferent to all .else but its issue.

This spirit, my dear Paddy, is moving me to employ every agency money can command for the recovery of little Mimi. I have just engaged the services of Jules Farman, per- haps the cleverest officer in Paris to-day, and he is with me .in this quest. Our latest call was upon the okl woman Marie, who lives in a cottage upon the great high road between Blois and Orleans. Here we gleaned but little. The child is the natural daughter of persons unknown. She .was left with a sum of money, and a "Mother's care "---do not laugh, Paddy—was bestowed upon her. Far- man assured me that this hag would not help us, but on the day following our return to Paris, he carizied me suddenly to the suburb of Rainey and declared that he had a clue. Mimi was travellin& with a rascally showman named Gondre. A-hundred franc note would buy her freedom—that freedom I would have paid not a hundred but ten thousand francs to ensure.
We left for Rainey early in the afternoon and visited the show as any bumpkins ready to gape at aged Pantaloon, or to lay our offer- ings at thern feet of a rouged and battered Columbine.

The tents were pitched in a clearing of the wood near the village—half a dozen of them with sorry spavined hacks grazing round about, and as fine a collection of rascality in charge as all Prance could show you. I will not dwell upon the shame with which I dis- covered myself seeking the child in these haunts. I am not easily moved to excite- ments, Paddy, but when we approached this place and I told myself that little Mimi had left rae for such a life as this, that I was about to re-discover her and take her to My house—bc sure never to leave it again—then, believe me, I lived one of the truest hours of life that I-have ever known.

I say that we walked about the ground a? ordinary bumpkins, but, be sure, our eyes were seeking Mimi everywhere, and the first 'disappointments came when we discovered nothing whatever that would justify Farman's optimism. - The.man Gondre proved to be a veritable clown of the vulgarest kind—a Id- low of small physique, mean eyes and jaded energies. He stood upon the platform of a booth supposed to contain an angry panther, who shared a dinner with a white-haired Cir- cassian, and generally displayed tenderness towards her—but *hen we paid our money and went in, we discovered the panther to be nothing more than a German wolf- hound, while the white-haired Circassian was a lady from the neighbourhood of la Galette, who had resorted with some success to the potentialities of common washing soda. This did not ,surprise me, but I was disap- pointed to find that Farman was well known to these people, and that I had done better to have gone •there alone. True, every door opened at his coming, but the suspicion re- mained that these vulgar- nits were being played against his own, and .that they under- stood perfectly well why he had come to Rainey. From this moment I. myself, despaired of finding Mimi at all. Useless for Farman to tell me that she was bidden somewhere in the neighbourhood of the fete and that be would not leave without her. I began to believe that, our coming had been anticipated and Mimi removed. It is ivue that a gleam of hope. came. to me after dinner, when my friend asked me to go with him to a cottage a little way from the town, and did not hesitate to say that Mimi was there. The place proved to be a tumble-down shanty in the very heart of the wood, a mere cabin reeking Of filthy odours and indescribably damp. Here we found the fellow Gondre, and with him a handsome girl, sleek and- dark-eyed and of the gipsy blood. They received us civilly, and said that they believed that the young woman was dis- covered and would be handed over to us. I perceived nothing in their demeanour to awaken suspicion, and for the. first. time I really dared to believe that Mimi was found. Farman, upon his part, took the affair a little cautiously. I think that he feared some- thing, both from the lonely situation of the house and the known reputation of those who owned it.
(To be Continued.)
ECZEMA. Nothing spoils a good disposition, Nothing taxes a man's patience, Like any irritation of the skin. Piles almost drive you mad. All day. they make you miserable.
All night tliey kt)e.l7 you awake.
Just tile same- with Cczema.
