div.head: CHAPTER X.
div.p: CHAPTER X.

[Henry Gastonard writes to Paddy O'Con- nell a letter concerning his search for Mimi the Simpleton.] Hotel St. Paul, Paris. July 15th, 1905. Dear Paddy,—The calamity of your sud- den departure from Paris is in no way miti- gated by the sad news I have to tell you. Mimi is not found. nor have I any clue to her whereabouts other than n. pitiful little letter from her, posted three days ago at Rainey, a ,suburb of Paris, and evidently a sincere expression of her determination not to return to me.

That Lea d'Alencon is at the bottom of it all I have not the smallest doubt. But there are subsidiary reasons, and one of them your own frankness before Mimi concerning my fortune and my future. The idea has come to her that I am lost if I remain in Paris. She is madly jealous of the other woman, and would have me leave France that I may also be quit of the fascinating Lea. Such is the truth, Paddy; 'such is the naive confession of one whom few would credit with so sure an instinct or so faithful an affection.

Meanwhile, as I need not tell you, who stood by me during the dark of the day, that my efforts to find her and to bring her back are unceasing, and pursued with all the ad- vantage my fortune can 'bestow. Recently, I revisited the old haunts at Neuilly, which we' re-discovered together before your sister's unfortunate illness recalled you from Paris. The quest of the lion-tamer, this horrible monster of a Catssadore, was rewarded with iuccess somo days ago. when I found him in a booth at Conflans, and was immediately ad- mitted to his' august presence. But be knows nothing of Mimi, nor is it reasonable to sup- pose that even her resolution would carry her again to scenes so reminiscent of the phantoms of her childhood. I say that he knows nothing of Mimi, but this is not to believe that he would not hear of her gladly, and press her joyfully to his grimy Ip-Asom if any opportunity occurred. A truly heroic figure. vast and proud and formidable, I found him in a wooden shed behind a crazy circus, taking a plat du jour of black bread and ancient beef, and making frequent applications to a green bottle which contained an unknown but, I doubt not, potent liquor. Upon either side were lions, which so delight the simple. people of the fetes and fairs about Paris. They were shut off from the passage in which be sat by huge beams of timber; but these stood so wide apart that a paw could pass at half a dozen places—and you, Paddy, will _ understand how much I enjoyed that interview. For thete were lions at the front of me and lions at the back of me,• and, although some of them seemed half asleep, there were others very wide awake indeed, and so playful that I wonder I came away Ivith any flesh upon my bones at all. _

We spoke _ between the roaring —no nleasant sound at any time, and doubly fear- ful when you have a lion 'within a foot of you. I found Cassadore quite frank, both about Mimi and his business. The lions, he admitted, were half - drugged when he put them through their paces. It was true that the great African brute Salambo had eaten his keeper, "Sammy," when he, Cassadore, was away in Paris; but; after all, you can- not make 'Christians of lions by burning them with . red-hot irons, nor was the "Sammy" aforesaid quite sober when he en- tered the .cage. In a voice resounding with dramatic tones, the man described how he had returned to find his servant eaten to the very neck—"mais, monsieur, the eyes were wide open and staring, and the head was untouched." Of Mimi the fellow told me much. He had bought her of ' an old woman at Orleans. There was no other wora for it. He saw the child capering before a dirty home, and was struck by the readiness and the wit with which she answered his questions. Assuming her to be a waif and stray entrusted by callous parents to a mercenary hag, he made a bargain on the spot, and took 'Mimi away with him. His

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S LETTER.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S LETTER.
Industrial Conditions in France.
NATIONAL DEFENCE.
(ConCenued from Last Week).
Before concluding this part of my letter may I just refer to a report of

INDUSTRIAL LIFE IN FRANCE —a companion volume to a similar report on Ger- many—just issued by the Board of Trade. These two volumes are largely the work of a. very patient and impartial investigator, the late Mr. Wilson Fox, and they cannot be challenged on the ground of any parti pris on his part or on the part of his colleagues. Indeed as the West- minster Gazette (from which I will briefly quote the summary of some extremely _important 4ures) points out if confirmation is wanted it will be found in the reports of the Tariff Com- mission ' itself, where it is shown with perfect candour that the chief complaint of the British manufacturer who wants Protection is just this —that his competitor abroad pays lower wages both to mechanics and labourers though they have to work longer hours, arid live at a lower standard of comfort. Let us then compare these figures showing how wages and hours of work and cost of living compare as between France and England, and Germany arid England. The Board of Trade report shows that

THE FRENCHMAN WORKS 17% LONGER HOURS AND YET EARNS ON THE LONGER NVEEK 25% LESS WAGES, AND HE THERE- FORE ACTUALLY EARNS 36% LESS FOR EACH HOUR'S WORK THAN HIS ENGLISH RIVAL. AND YET ON THE OTHER HAND HE HAS TO PAY 18% :10RE FOR HIS WEEKLY BUDGET IF FUEL IS INCLUDED.
So much for France,a country of great natural wealth and resources, but with a highly devel- oped protective system. Take the other great- industrial competitor of ours in Europe.
THE GERMAN WORKMAN PAYS 23% MORE FOR RENT AND 15% MORE FOR HIS FOOD, AND YET HE RECEIVES 17% LESS WAGES, ALTHOUGH HE HAS TO WORIC 11% LONGER HOURS.

Of course, Tariff Reformers tell us thcy have no idea of imposing a high duty like that which has been adopted in France and Germany. Yes, the democracies of these countries were told just the same pretty tale when protection was first started there. Duties on flour which began at 6d. per cwt. in France and 1/- per cwt. in Ger- many were increased by gradual stages to 6/6 per cwt. in France and 5/- per cwt. in Germany. The duties on meat began at 1/- per cwt. in France and mounted up to 30/-; those duties beginning at 13/- in Germany mounted up to 37/6. The reason is simple enough. When the promises with which Protectionists in the first place tickled the cars of people are not realised at once, there is a cry for more Protection as the remedy, and we have abundant evidence that that would be precisely the course things in England would take. Mr. Balfour, the decoy duck, as he has been termed, of the Unionist party it is well- known heartily detests such Protection as the whole-hoggers are aiming at. His position was brilliantly hit off the other day by one .of the shrewdest observers in the House here. He remarked, if Balfour gets into power again, what he wants to do is to "give his party the thinnest of thin slices of Tariff Reform—cut from the whole hog." Yes, that is what Mr. Balfour wants, but not at all what his party wants or will allow. That obscure band of somewhat obscure men known as the Confederates, arc in league with the friends of monopoly in this country—those who would be ready enough if in a rash and reckless moment the chance were ever given them to insist on a .full-blooded policy of Pro- tcction under which they would sacrifice the interests of the public so as to rapidly grow rich at their expense. I am already trespassing unduly on your space and it would not be proper to prolong this letter by entering in detail into the discussion of

THE NAVAL ESTIMATES we have had this week. It would lam sure also be superfluous to do so because those debates on this question of supreme importance will as- suredly have been followed day by day this week in Warrington. Let me just mention the opin-, ions formed and confirmed in one's mind. during the progress of a debate which one has naturally followed closely. First of all under difficult circumstances and at a critical time I think the Government have come to a most vise decision in the course they have decided to take. Mr. Mc Kenna dealt with the Government's position and policy in a speech of much precision, such as one expects from a man of his mathematical turn of mind. No ex- ception could be taken to- the tone of Mr. Bal- four's reply, but* I think it has been clearly demonstrated in the debate that he took an exaggerated view of things, and indeed that he has been Misled as to matters of fact.

Therefore in the second place I do not think hc has made good his position; while as to Mr. Lea, and all his talk about a one-power standard, I think he goes perilously near the position of an irresponsible panic-monger. There is no ques- tion of a one-power standard or anything approaching it. Our Superiority over Germany on the water to-day is overwhelming, and in 1912 we shall still have, as of course we are bound to maintain, an immense preponderance of power on the high seas. . In the third place, while one can well under- stand how many economists of the old school de- test this increase of expenditure, and while indeed we must all deeply lament it, I cannot agree with the views put forward by some idealists here who arc apparently willing to take risks which this country neither will consent to run, nor ought to run. Ido not believe for a moment that any responsible German is at the present time seriously contemplating the invasion of this country ; all this talk about imminent invasion is to my mind a wild chimera. But we must take heed for the future as well as for the present day. At the present time, besides a very natural desire to have adequate protection for her very large over-sea trade—which Would otherwise be entirely at our mercy—besides that I have not a "doubt .that by forcing the pace as she has done Germany has had a shrewd notion that the nearer she can get to our naval power, the more emphatically will she be able to underline her diplomatic notes to us and to others, and so, it is a question of degree, and what I feel after this three days' debate is that the Government have acted with wisdom and good judgment. . In the fourth. place, I feel, if:possible More strongly than ever the immensely important factor that the

NEW TERRITORIAL FORCE is ,and will be in thc defence of the country. . AS I have before said and written, I believe also that both directly and indirectly, this force will to a not inappreciable extent in the future help to check increase in naval and military expen- diture. It is a great mistake for people to talk of the Territorials as Mere food for foreign powder should they ever be brought face to face with foreign conscripts. What must be remembered is this, that if ever the utterly im- probable did happen, and this country were in- vaded the invaders would be met by our regular soldiers. Stiffened in the back by the' presence ' of the regulars, I will be bound the .Territorials _would give a mighty good account of them- selves, and the enemy being utterly outnumbered, and with its base of _supply cut off by , our navy, would be starved into .surrender. 'know it is said that invaders would seize their opportunity to attack us when our regular army was engaged in some serious foreign war, hit if any such ' critical time ever arrived, long before this country was denuded, or anything like denuded of a powerful force of regulars, the Territorials would be called out for their six months' train- ing, and at what would then be a time of national emergency would readily respond ; and though I am not a military man myself I can quote the opinion of high military authorities like Generals French and lan Hamilton, who are satisfied that after such training the Terri- torials would make things very hot for any invader. Asa civilian I am not in any position to dogmatise on a matter of this kind, but if I may Offer my opinion for what it is worth, then I say that apart from numerical superiority which would be considerable, I believe that malt for man the Territorials would be fully a match

for the foreigner. For these reasons, and for every reason, one is thankful to hear that th,e country is responding well /to Mr. Haldane s appeal. Recruiting goes on apace, and one was glad to read in the Manchester Guardian NO at Mr. Haldane was able to say of East Lancashire , in his recent visit to Cottonopolis. This summer the King comes to visit Lanca- , shire. Let us hope that by that time Lancashire ' as a whole will play a foremost part in England . in support of the Territorials, and Warrington a foLTmost part in Lancashire. In the fifth place, to talk of an understand- ing with Germany at present on the matter of armaments may seem woefully mistimed, but it , is just as well to remember how strained rela- tions with other nations have given place to a much better state of affairs, and sooner or later . ---4 he would be a rash man who ventured to pre- ' dict which at the present time—we 'must look forward to the time when we can come to ati understanding with Germany. The question of terms opens a field which I cannot enter at the end of so long a letter, for the inordinate length of which indeed I must apologise to you and yonr _ readers.—Yours, etc.,
A. H. CROSFIELD.

P.S.—I have dictated this letter rather late this evening and I shall not have an opportunity. to revise it before it catches to-night's post, and must therefore beg to be excused if there are any verbal errors, or errors of punctuation. As it happens I was in the same position a fortnight since, and one or two errors did consequently crop up in my letter then. I cannot resist the temptation of adding just a. word about last night's debate. We did have such a gooil time; indeed, Liberals and Free Traders in all parts of the House thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Churchill was in top fighting form, and at such a time he is an awkward- man to tackle, as Balfour and poor "Austen" found to their cost. They had beet! setting up the latest Tariff Reform fetish in the market place labelled "Export of Foreign Capital,' and -Churchill, in his ruthless and remorseless way, broke it to pieces before their eyes. By the way, I notice that Earl Winterton was offering homage to the same fetish in Warring- ton this week. Weil, it is one thing to talk Tariff Reform on a platform to a sympathetic audience, but a very different thing to trot out its fallacies where they can be met and answered, as they are answered across the table in the House, and so I am afraid both Mr. Bal- four and Austen Chamberlain had an unhappy time of it, and arc wishing to-day they had not spoken.—A. H. C. 18th March, 1909.

div.head: MANURING POTATOES.
div.p: MANURING POTATOES.

So many experiments have been made in the manur- ing of potatoes that there is now little doubt as to the best treatment—NTiz., a moderate dressing of farmyard manure, supplemented by a complete mixture of artiflcials. The dung is very beneficial says " Farm and Home," because of its mechanical action, but the feeble-rooting potato requires some soluble manures ready for its use during the early period of growth. The farmyard manure—say, 6 to 12 tons per acre—is best ploughed hi during autumn or early spring, but IS sometimes given in the drills. The artiticials should always be given in the drills, the seed-tubers being dropped right on top of the manure. A typical dress- ing of artificials may consist of 3 cwt. superphosphate 1!, cwt. sulphate of ammonia, and 11 cwt. sulphate or murinte of potash per acre, though sometimes 2 cwt. of the first ingredient and 1 cwt. each of the others Is enough.

ODDFELLOWSIIIP.—A social evening in connection with the" Navigatic " Lodge was held at the" (leach end Horses " Hotel on Saturday evening, when there was a large attendance of menAels including Lot Brooks, P.G.M. G. P. Freeman, P.D. O.M. T. P. Fortes, - P.P.G.M 's T. P. Bradshaw, %V. Helbrook, Frank Webster (C.S.), T. Blackl.urn (Eccles). Bros. T. Harris (Swansea), J. A. Wright, IV. Dennett, T. Newnes, A. Marsh, W. Ashton, J. Fairlinrst, J. Swift and others. Noble Grand Wood proposed a hearty welcome to the District OfEcers.—Alcer several songs and toasts were given the Grand Master of the Warrington District (Bro. G. F. Freeman) made a presentation of a P.P.G.M,'s gold=jewel to P.P.G.I. Lot Brooks for his services to the District and said he was indeed honoured by baying, the privilege in doing so know ing as be did the excellent work rendered to the District and Lodges by Bro. Brooks. In reviewing the past work of Fit o. Brooks he remirided the brothers present aat the recipient had Tasted through the District choirs of his lodge four times,heenr lecture master, and had attended.on all com- mittees thereby establishing the fact that he bad sacrificed much time to help the sick and &stressed and to further the good objects of the Society. He hoped that all the members would take a pattern of the good work &me and trusted that Bro. Brooks w onld have long life to wear the beautiful jewel, and that Mr. Brooks , and fanrily would appreciate it a recompense for his absence from home on busines3, in cc nnection with the Order. (Loud applause). Brother Broekes (who was received saith musical honours) replied in an apprecia- live speech arid said be would do all in his power to carry on the good work and thanked the members for their kind reward of his efforts. (Applause). Brothers J. P Bradshaw, W. Holbrook, F'erank Webster, J. A. Wright, W. Ashton, T. Harris and T. Blackburn elso spoke. Songs were well rendered by Brothers T. P, Forbes, W. Dennett and others and a recitation given by Brother Harris. Brother J. Swift acted as pianist.

Penketh and Sankey. A LANTERN LECTURE.—The Penketh and Sankey branch of the British and Foreien Bible Society held their annual rceeting in the Friends' School lecture, Stock's-lane, on Monday at 'La).- r. W. E. Brown was in the chair and WAS supported on the platform by Mrs. Robert, Garnett, who acts as local secretary, the Rev. J. Gunnell, and the Rev. W. Houghton, .the lecturer. Mrs. Garnett gave an account of the work in the dis- trict. The amount contributed the. district was £l3. She would like to sea it increased and 'would be pleased to wait on anyone who wished to contribute.—Mr. Houghton gave a most interesting lecture on the work in Siberia bird Manchuria which was appreci tel by all present, the leas being excellent. Mr. R,thinsin manipulated the lantern.At theclos3 Mr.J.G.Wiehinshaw proposed a vole of thanks to Mr. Houghton for his lecture and Mr. Broun for the use of the lecture Mr. Jenks seconded and the proposil wai carried with enthusiasm.

LABOUR PARTY.—The local Lahoar Party held a meeting in one of the rooms at the Wesleyan scho.ds last Friday.—The President (Mr. S. Faulkner) was in the chair, and in his opening remarks said he was pleased to see so many pres.nt, ti take part. in the dis- cussion, and in a rousing address hoped the m,mbers would increase. He was stare the electors in the Nect ton Division had a good man in Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., a man ho did his bast for the workers, aud in using the woid "workers" he meant those who worked with their ',rains as well as those who did manual labour. He urged each one present to do his best to increase !he membership !of the party so as to send Mr. Seddon to Parliament at, the next election. Mr. Haley from Warrington thea spoke, and said if the conitades wanted a subject to debate he would recommend them the subject of unemployment.- In giving his experience of the various deputations lie had been on for the unemployed be said he bad found a great deal of sympathy, in fact.that am about all be bad found. The address had a great effect on the meeting and from the tone of the gath-qin4 !Lord Wolmer will have thtoy questions of a knotty character to answer when he comes to Penketh.
Stockton If oath. STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY. GRAND SHOW OP FLOWERS.

At the Stockton-Heath annual flower and bulb show on Saturday the air was " alive " with the perfume, for bundreda of spring, fiewers, Kph as hyacinths, daffodilg tulips and nareiSsi, told one that glorous spring I:ad really come. An excellent show was made of both the hyacinthe and daffodils. A fine collection which was not for competition was sent- by the President (Sir Gilbeit Greened', Bart.) Attractive exhibits were also sent by, Mr. Vere B. Davies (vice- president), the Rev. J. Collins, and Alderman Bolton. There was a large attendance at the opening ceremony, which took place at 3 o'clock in the afternoon, being performed by Mrs. Armitaae, of Walton Lea. Mr. Vero B. Davi s,' presided. Mr. Davies regretted that their President (Sir Gilbert Greenall) was away from home and could not be present,and said it crave him great pleasure to preside at the first show of the year. There had been some talk of giving up the bulb show, but he thought they would agree that the display that -day justified its con- tinuation. It would interest them to know that there wete 59 exhibitors and 160 exhibits this year as against 16 exhibitors and 39 exhibit.s last !ear,(Applause),lt was his honoura,ile and pleesatit duty to ask Mrs. Armitage to open the show and be ext. nded-to tier a hearty eleiime. That was her first appearance in publio at Stockton Heath and he hoped it would not be her last. Mrs. Armitage bad Wildly promised to gke a prize or pr:zes in eonae shape or form. (Applause). Mrs. Armitage in opening the show said that before coinine to live at Walton Lea she had occasibn to pass through Stockton He7th almost daily during the latter pr.rt of the season, and the one thing that impressed itself upon her, was the brightness of the gardens and the evident care and attention which bad been bestowed upon them. When Mr. 1' awcett asked her to open the show she was very pleased indeed to take a small part in the work, the result of which she appreciated. She was glad to notice the efforts made to interest the juveniles in the cultivation of flowers. for on them the tenure of the Steckten Heath Garden Society naturally ,depended. Stu.. had gnat pleasure in declaring the bulb show open. (Applause). Mr. C. ilbitss•roal in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage, urged the importance of making the ,pring show a pre-eminently successful one. He strenn- pesty opposed any sugt °et ion of discontinuing the bulb shoe s,aed was glad such a course bad met with oppoSition. Great interest was now being tal en in the cultivation f (lowers and plants by the school ch'leiren in different manu,sactuiing towns. The Garden Society had a gooil tany lady friends and they were extremely delighted t welcome M's. friends, who they believed would be another friend. (Appliarse). Rey. J. Coilins briefly seconded and the motion was passed with unanimity. A handsome bouquet Was then presented to Mrs. Armitage by Miss MeDermid. Mr. Armitage, in responding on behalf-of his wife, said it was a pleasure to go among enthusiasts in a cause in which one was specially 'interested. The greater the intercourse the greater was the development of lovJ of the com- munity, love of the parish and the greatest was the development of pitriotisni which was the chief need of our country to-day. Mrs. Armitage and himself greatly appreciated the work they had done and were proud to be able to tal:e a small share in assisting to further their aims. LOCAL WILL—The will of the late Mr. T. F. Holliwell, of the Plough Hotel, Lymm, near Warring- ton' Las been proved at £1,303.

- HOCKEY.—LYMM LADIES V. CROSFIELD'S LADIES CLUB.—This match was played at Lynrm on Saturday and resulted after a game which through want of cohesion was of a very scrappy character in a draw, no goals being scored. MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.—The committee net OD Tuesday night and decided to hold the coronation on Whit Thursday. A satisfactory response to the canvass for subscriptions has enabled the committee of volun- tary workers to come to this decision. When given fine weather and the heart x seconding of their efforts by the inhabitants the affair should be equal to anything Eit the sort held in the county. The secretaries we Messrs. F. W. Ashton and H. S. Saville, jun., and Mr. George Willan is the treasurer. ='

BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the Lymm branch of this society was held last Friday evening the 19th inst. in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom. The President of the branch, , Rev. G. B. Thurston, M.A. in the chair. The hen. treasurer, Mr.F. 0. Moston, gave his report, and sub- mitted his accounts which compared very favourably with last year's. The officers for the current year were duly elected :—President, Rev. G. B. Thurston, M.A. treasurer, Mr. F. 0. Moston ; hon. secretary, Mr. D. Mort. After the business portion of the .meeting was concluded a very interesting lecture illustrated by lime light views w'as given by the society's Manchester representative, Rev. T. A. Wolfendale, M.A. The, title of the lecture was" Through Siberia and Manchuria to Port Arthur." Mr. W. T. Moss very kindly manipulated the lantern. . OUGHTRINCTON ST. PETER'S v. ALTRINGHAM TEhIPLARS. A.F.C. MEDAL COMPETITION-- This replayed tie—the previous attempt being a drawn game. —was played on the ground of the first named on Saturday last. Goulding kicked off for the Ternplars and from a well-combined movement on the right wing Gregson centred well. The home full back in trying to clear unfortunately foulded Coulding, a penalty ensuing from which that player regis:ered a goal. St. Peter's, stimulated by this reverse now warmed to their work. Some good play in which Rouse and A. Hutt were prominent was seen. Gresty for St. Peters centred well, enabling Lord to put in some good rasping shots, but without success. Give and take play followed which culminated in Gregson after a fine individual effort scoring goal number two for the Templars. Half-time arriving with the score: Templars, 2; St. Peter's, o.—The second half opened sensationally the 'hall being rushed down the field by St. Peter's, and Barnet only partially clearing Shaw nipped in and scored number one for St. Peter's. The Templars now seemed to go to pieces the Oughtring- ton team being all over them with the result that Lord, Simpson, Gresty, and Briars succumbed in getting past their defence. Time being called with the score : Oughtrington St. Peter's, •5 • goals ;. Altrincham Ternplars, 2 goals. CANAL MYSTERY.—Mr. T: Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at Ls,-mm on Wednesday morning on the body__ of an unknown man which was found floating in the canal on Monday.—James Nicholls, a carter resid- ing in Sandy-lane, stated that about 5 pan. on the day in question he was going for a load of slack, and on passing over .Dog's Bridge, he saw the body floating in the canal, on the Lynim side of the bridge. Witaess took the tens off his horse and pulled the body to the side. With the aid of a censtable the body was taken from the water.—P.C. Herbert Dodd, stationed at Lyrom, said that he received informational:mut 5 p.m. on Monday afternoon as to a body being in the canal. He proceeded there and with the aid of the last witness conveyed the body to Mr. Leigh's shed. The man appeared to be about 30 years of age, and was 5-it. Oin. in height. lie had a fresh complexion, with dark brown hai,. [he body was in a shocking cond‘Con, the left arm and tight heed being broken and the head badly damaged. Deceased was almost devoid of clothing, there being a piece of blue serge on the right leg. He was wearing pair of cotton socks, a pair of good bootsw;th" Perfect Models" and Every Comfort " stamped upon them ; and also a collar and tie. There was a laundry mark on the collar 'but it was not r( coguisable. The body appeared to have been in the water for 10 or 11 (lays. A verdict "Found Drowned " was returned.— The question arose of providing a mortuary at Lyrnrn, One juryman remarking. that the shed at present used was entirely unsuitable for the purpose.—lt was decided to write to tie Urb in District Council on the ruatter.—The Coroner sain he entirely' agreed with the jury ; it was very objectionable for pniple to have to go into the shed in order to identify their dead.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT THE WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT THE WESLEYAN CHURCH.

There was a very pretty wedding at the Weslesan Church, Lymm, on Wednesday when Mr. Frank- Pickton Brown, son of Mr. and Mts. Edwin Brown, Brentwood, Lymm, was married to Miss Annie Winstanley, fourth daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Winstanley, Ryecroft, Ls mni. The bride and bridegroom are toth well-known in the 'district and a large congregation assembled to witness the ceeemony. The chancel was tastefully decorated with choice plants und flowers. The service was Con- ducted by the Rev. Thomas Gladding. The full choir was in • attendance and the hymns" The Voice that breathed o'er Eden" and "0 Father all (renting" were sung. Mr. M. Eastham, Porthleven, Lymm, was at the organ and played suitable selections, including Mendelesohn's "Wedding March.' rhe bride, who as givtn away by ber,father, was cliarm:ngly attired in a gown of silk eolienne, with net veil and wreath of orange blessomornd carried a lovely bouquet of orchids end lilies, presented by Mr. Champ, Foxley Hense, Lymm. • Her ornament was a gold curb, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaid, Miss Eva Winstanley, wore a pretty dress of old rose shade silk eolienne, with hat to match, and her bouquet was composed of pink cernations. She also wore a .gold caul), presented by the bridegroom. Mr. Fred Champ, of foxley House. discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremony a reception was held at lisecroft, and later the newly- married couple left for Derby shire where the honeymoon is being spent. Many lie-tuti ful, Presents were received including a massive inkstand from the members of the Wesleyan choir, Wesley Guild, and the Sunday school (with which the bride and bridegroom have been con- nected all their lives), and a handsome inlaid Sheraton clock, with inscription, from the members of the Lyinin Choral Society of which the bridegroonf has hem secretary since its forftat ion.

div.head: Grappenhall.
div.p: Grappenhall.
THE ADJOURNED PARISH MEETING.

There was a large attendance at the adjourned parish meeting on Thursday, the parish councillors present being Mr. A. L. Kaye, Mr. G. Ashton and Mr. Laurence Bolton, with Mr. C.H. Huult (clerk). Mr.S. Jenkins was not present. Mr. Kaye refused to take the chair, and on the nomination of Mr. J. B. Parkhouse, Mr. Beresford Melville presided.

div.head: JOHNSON CHARITY FUND.
div.p: THE JOHNSON CHARITY FUND.

The Chairman explained that although not conversant with the whole of the proceedings of the Council in the matter of the Johnson Charity Fund, he did know that the fund was for relief and had been administered by the Rector and churchwardens of Grappenhall to he poor of Grapp(nhall, Christ Church and St. James', atchford, and that in the tpinion of the Charity Commission whose report they had had the Fund bad been properly administered. He suggested and recom- mended that the meeting approve of the Parish Council's decision at the last meeting. The Clerk explained that in 1698 a certain farm rent of £l4 per annum in the name of trustees had been left to provide the Johnson Charrty Fund on a lease of 2,000 years. A resolution was then pub to the meeting that the Council's decision be approved and bias carried by a large majority.

div.head: EATING OF SMALL TENEMENTS.
div.p: EATING OF SMALL TENEMENTS.

The Clerk read a proposition of April 10th, 1008, pur- porting that it, was desirable that the Council should adopt the old system of the non-compounding of rates. At that time the proposition was not, seconded and the matter was dropped. Mr. Fairburat asked if much loss was sustained by tenants paying theirovvnratesin largely populated dis- trict 4 it was considerable.

The Clerk said there was not much lose, but in several cases he had traced Several removals without avail and of course in such cases he had no remedy against the proper owner under the present system. _ .
was decided, how-ever, to retain the existing system of compounding.
VICTORIA-ROAD.
Mr. N. Cook draw the attention of the Council to Victoria-road. He said it was in a very undesirable condition.

Mr. Bolton said that the Victoria-road making had been under the constant consideration of the District Council for the past nine- months. It had • been con- sidered that the gradient of 1 in 40 yards was a draw- back to making the road one of tarred macadam,but seeing that there was not very much traffic it had been decided to make a 'road of that description in spite of the gradient. _ _ _ _ _

- !Ur. Parkhouse thought that some delay might yet be experienced if the consent of the property owners bad not yet been got. Mr. B olton The property owners have themselves already petitioned for the road, and the work would he put in hand almost immediately. PRIVATE ROADS (?) Mr. Fairhurst moved: That it be a recommendation to the Parish Council to make enquiries about the foot- paths in the parish and ascertain under what conditions they were used—whether they were public or private roads.
Mr. Leach seconded, and it was carried unanimously.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
SCHOOLGIRL'S STRAN CE DEATH.

Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquiry at the Widnes Police Station on Saturthy touching the death or Florence Locke, the ten-year-old dattphter of Henry Locke, of 47, Grensell-street. It transpired tlurt the deteised, who was a delicate child from birt,h,.cmc hOme from school on Thursday 'afternoon, and lit Pst. playing marbles she fell down and complained of pains in her back. Shea- tal,en to pr. flutchin,on, nho examined Ler and precrihed for a (old. lie could find no symptons of any other ailment.. She wms ca.ried home and put to bed, where she was found dead next mosning. _

Dr: Hu'chinson slid be wAs surprised to hear of her death, and wrote to the coroner UAL he did n it know the cause of death, and wis at a lo.s to acaount for The coroner orcbred a pot-tno!tern exlminition, the result of which was that •it was fount the child was very delicate. There were no marks of violenc. div.head: GOLDEN CITY BAZAAR.
div.p: GOLDEN CITY BAZAAR.
PICTURESQUE SCENE IN THE PARR HALL. -- Opening By Mrs. Lloyd-George. -- MR. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P. AND _ THE NAVAL SCARE.

As if by the touch of a magic wand; the Parr Hall lias this week been transformed into a scene of, Oriental splendour. Graceful domes and minarets of gold, a magnificent floral palace with terraces and flower gardens, with here and there a glimpse of "eastern aky "—on canvas, of course—make up a picturesque "Golden City." .A more suitable title for a bazaar could hardly have been chosen, and it is the hope of the Baptists cif Warrington that the " city " will be golden in more senses than one, for in the quaint courts and shops there is a varied display of beautiful wares to be disposed of, the high ambition of the , bazaar promoters being to raise a sum of at least £l,OOO to enable them to secure a promised grant of £5OO for the erection of a Baptist Central Hall which will take the place of the present,church in Golborne- street. For, months past the members of the church have worked with commendable zeal to ensure the success of the project and,looking round the Parr Hall on Wednesday, they had every reason to be proud of their handiwork. Rarely has such a pleasing spectacle been presented at a local bazaar and the useful and ornamental goods were so alluringly set out on the stalls that visitors found it hard to resist the invita- tions to purchase. Warrington Baptists have an honourable history reaching back to the dim past, for we find a Baptist church here at the time of the Civil Wars. They have passed through many vicissitudes but the prospects were never brighter than they are at present. Under the leadership of the Rev. R. E. Letheren much head- way is being made, and it is felt that the time for a great forward step has arrived. The existing premises are almost a hundred years old and the accommoda- tion both for church and school purposes is( very -unsatisfactory. It has therefore been decided to build a Central Hall, comprising new church and schools and suitable adjuncts, at an estimated cost of £3,000. The provision of new school-premises has been in Con- templation for a considerable time, and with this object in view, money has been set aside at Varicus times, with the result that there is now in hand a sum of over £3OO. As a result of representations made to the Baptist Union concerning the position of the 'church in Warrington, a grant of £5OO was allocated by the Twentieth Century Fund towards the building of a new church. By the terms of this grant, the promise expires in June, 1009 -and the purpose in holding the bazaar, is to raise the sum of at .least £lOOO to put the church in a position to secure this promised grant, and to commence building this spring. - With such a commendable object in view, the Golden City bazaar, is naturally regarded as a red letter and even epoch-making event in the life of the church, and that it meets with the. sympathy of the leaders of the denomination is evident from the fact that the veteran Rev. Alexander McLaren sent a most cordial message of good-will, stating how much he admired the faith and coubge which animated Mr. Lethren and his friends. The-bazaar opened on Wednesd'ay and will con- tinue until this (aturday) evening. Ro effort has been spared to make it as attractive as possible and there is such an admirable series of entertainments that even those who are inclined to esdiew the usual type of sale of work are able to spend a very pleasent time.

div.head: STALLTIOL DE RS.
div.p: THE STALLTIOL DE RS.

The following is a list of the stall-holders : CHURCH AND CONGREGATIONAL STALL—Mesdames Clatworthy (secretary), Few (treasurer), J. S. Hughes, Hankey, Pcpper, Wilson, E. W. Jones, H. Buckby, Shackles, Freeman, Tynan, Longshaw, Barnett, Bowden, Hawthorne, Heywood, Mansell, Littlewood, Jones and Hamer, and Miss Richards. r BAZAAR STACL (at which the Women's Circle had promised to raise £loo).—Girls' Section : Mrs. Edgar Balmford, assisted by the younger members. Mothers' Union: Mrs. John Starkey, assisted by the mothers. China Supplement : Mrs. Dunn, Mrs. Wood, the Misses I Roberts, assisted by the hon. associates. THE BROTHERHOOD STALL.— Se cret aries,: Mr. Pepper and Mr. W. Heywood. Financial : Mr. T. S. I Davies, Mr. W.. Stevens. Soap and Perfume: Mr. G. Hall. SUNDAY SCHOOL STALL—Mr. S. Fernley (superin- tendent), Mesdames Fernlev (Convenor)W.Woods, Rice, and G. 'Misses L. Heywood (treasurer), Hankey. C. Hankey, Richardson, Barnett, M. Freeman,,pd Green. ART NEEDLEWORK AND ART POTTERY STALL— lisses Fieldhouse, Misses Pickavance, Misses Balm- ford, Miss Dodds, Miss Elsie Bailey, and Miss Agatha Jones. BAND OF Hon STALL—Patron, Mrs. J. Mirror), Stockport; Misses Bate, Sharples,Jackson,and Richards, Mesdames R. Nelson, G. Whitfield, Whitmore, Shaw, Ormiston, J. Monks, Messrs. J. Muir (convenor), A. Few (secretary). A. Hunt (treasurer), R. Nelson, G. Whitfield, and J. Monks. Scorrisx STALL—Mesdames Muir, Eddleston and Ellison, Misses B. E. llolden, G. Holden and Mclver. DAIRY AND PRODUCE STALL—M rS. Billington and friends, Mrs. Elwell and Mrs. Bradley. PHOTOGRAPHIC STALL (devoted to the Works of Mr. James Parkinson, who is kindly giving the takings to the bazaar funds).—Miss Annie M. Roberts. REFRESH MENT STALL.—Mesdames E. Lloyd-Jones, England and Sherburn. OFFICERS OF THE BAZAAR. The following were the officers of the bazaar : Treasurer, %tr. J. A. Longland ; financial secretary, Mr. W. Clatworthy ; organising secretary, Mr. R. Roberts; general secretary, Mr. T.Longshaw. OPENING BY MRS. LLOYD-GEORGE. MR. CROSFIELD AND THE NAVY SCARE.

Special interest centred in the first day's proceedings as Mrs. Lloyd-George, wife of the Chancellor of the Exchequer,attended to perform this opening ceremony. The large attendance anforred well for the success of the bazaar. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., presided and amongst others on the platform -were :—Mrs. Lloyd- George, Revs. R. E. Letheren, J. S. Hughes and J. B. Bugloss, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman fwd. Mrs. Forshaw), Mrs. Letheren, Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Proker, Mrs. Dodds, Mrs. Garnett, Mrs. Congreve. Mrs. P. RylandA, Mrs. C. J. Holmes, Mrs. Osborne, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Locker, Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Pemberton. Mrs. Withinshaw, Mrs. Clegg, Mrs. Dutton. Mrs. Lindley, Miss Bessie Dot ton,Miss Morrison,Miss Short,Alderrnan Ellison, Mr. J. Lorgland, Mr. E. Wynne-Jones, and the bazaar officials. The Rev. R. E. LETHEREN read a letter from the Rev. J. J. Fitch, of Southport, Moderator of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches, regretting his inability to attend, and stating that it would have been a pleasure and pride to aim to have moved a vote of thanks to Mrs. Lloyd George.—Mr. James Dodds wrote "I regret I have an engagement for 2.30 on Wednesday which will prevent my having the honour of joining in the welcome to Mrs. Lloyd- George, which I hope will be as warm and enthusiastic as it ought to be, for her own sake as well as for that of her distinguished husband,from whom the country has had and from whom it confidently looks for many beneflcient reforms." Continuing, Mr. Letheren said he was sure he was speaking for all present as well as for himself when he offered a word of whole- hearted welcome to their distinguished visitor, Mrs Lloyd:George. (Applause.) As far as he and his own people were concerned, to say that she was welcome was too utterly weak to express a thousandth part of the thankfulness they felt for her presence. When they first heard she was corning it was not as though sunshines were merely added to day light; ale turned the shadow of night into -morning and -made their intry hearts break forth with something of the sunshine and the sense of spring. It was something like the service Blucher rendered to Wellington at Waterloo—Mrs. Lloyd-George had "raved the situation." (Laughter.) When he (Mr. Letheren) told them that their organis- ing secretary was a Welshman, they would understand why the first name \ to be mentioned in connection with the opening of the hazelr was that of the Baptist Chancellor of the Exchequer—the Right Hon. D. Lloyd-George. (Applause). They were not successful in persnading him to come and if they had cast their minds forward to the particular time of the year in which that bszaar was herd, they might, have known that Mr.Lloyd-George would probably be far too deeply interested in devising ways and means of getting money out of them than to he able to spare a day to come and help a few poor Baptist people to get a little money together. (Laughter). But high and distinguished as was the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer, how much higher and more important was the office of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's chan- cellor of the exchequer ! (Laughter and applause). Mr. Crosfield's name was a household word in Warrington. Ile (Mr. Letheren) believed he had seen it somewhere in close association with "Perfection." (Laughter). The interest which Mr. Cresfield had shown in their scheme , from the beginning, the kindly help which he had rendered at many a stage during its progress, the petsonal trouble and interest be had taken in arranging for the visit of Mrs. Lloyd-George, and his presence that day came es near to" perfectien "in friendly w, service as they were likely to meet with in their pilgrimage through this vale of tears. (Applause. Their only regret was that Mrs, Crosfield vvas not with them. Really they owed more to Mrs. Crosfleld's winsome persistence and her very skilful diplomacy in getting Mrs. Lloyd-George to come, than to anybody else. With regard to the object of the bazaar the new school bed teen in the air for twenty eare, and -the

object of that bazaar was to put a foundation under it. Owing to the existing trade depreasion and lack of employment they, bad fallen on a very unfortunate time, but they had done all they could, and be felt sure that those present were prepared to give them kind and generous help. (Applause). Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., said it was a very great pleasure to him to associate himself with all that Mr. Letheren had said, and although he could not express it quite as eloquently, nor yet as graphically, he was glad to have that opportunity of joining with Mr. Letheren and with Mr. Hughes too in giving a very hearty welcome, on behalf of all present, to their guest who had come down from London. (Applause:) "Allusion has been made," continued Mr. Crosfield, "to the other occupations that have prevented Mr. Lloyd-Geoege being with Us, and while there are at the present time absolutely incessant demands on the whole of his time and energy I do not need to tell you what demands there are also upon our good friend Ms. Lloyd George in assisting her distinguished husband and in helping to take careof him while he has this groat strain of work upon him. It will no doubt interest Mrs. Lloyd-George to know that it was from this very platform only a few years since that the gallant Welsh chief rain addressed us in Warrington. (Applause.) On that occasion not only Liberals and others of the progressive party but many Conservative friends of mine, I am happy to say, came to hear Mr. Lloyd-George, and lam sure I am only voicing the general opinion of the town when I say that of all the speeches that have ever been delivered in Warringtcn since our political history began, that great speech of Mr. Lloyd-George's will rank as one of the most signal, str:king and memorable. (Applause.) I should be tempted to make one or two quotations from it to-day, but then, you know, if I did that I should be verging at once upon politics— (laughter)—and I have a shtewd suspicion that this afternoon, at any rate, politics are strictly barred." (Laughter.) Continuing 'gr. Crosfield said that since Mr. Parr conferred the great boon upon Warrington of pre- senting thatfine hall, they had had visits from so many distinguished men of different shades of opinion that he thought they might already speak of that platform

work of our chapels, indeed our Free Churches in Wales are the very centre of our life, both spiritual and social, and I am very glad to see these Welshmen in Warrington partaking of the burden of the church here. When I look around on these beautiful stalls, laden with very tempting articles, they tell me of weeks and indeed of months of very bard work and self-sacrifice on the part of's great many members of the Church, everyone doing a share in his or her own way to work and collect all those things together. I very much hope that by the close of the bazaar you will reap the fruits of your labours, and that this undertaking will be a very great success indeed. Tbe lady stall- holders and their helpers are, I am sure, anxious to begin work; they have not come to stand idle, and they want at once to begin the dispogal of their articles. I feel certain they will make the best possible use of their opportunity, and I have now much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause). The MAYOR said he h.rd to propose a vote of thanks to the good wife of their worthy and excellent Chan- cellor of the Exchequer. (Applause.) Mr. Lloyd- George was also a worthy professional brother of his, and he was pleased to be able to call h;nr. such. (Applaitse.) It was a great pleasure to him to be present as Mayor of the borough and he was thank- ful to say that his mind was broad enough to honour real Christian earnestness wherever it appeared —(applause)—whether in the Church of England, the Baptist Church, the Roman Catholic Church or any other religious body. They were all aiming for the ' same goal and all their ministers were teaching them to serve their Heavenly King rightly as well as their eiribly King ond coontry. It was very kind of Mrs. Lloyd-George to come down to support them by her pre.eLce, and he hoped they would get everything they required. (Applause.) Mrs. LETHEREN, in seconding, said they had been threatened several times and from,. different sources with disappointment and failure, and when it was definitely announced that Mrs. Lloyd-George was coming it was as though the sun of promise and,success shone out brilliantly from the dark background ot doubts and fears. They ware told beforehand that Mrs. Lloyd-George was very charming, simple and unaffected

div.head: VIEW OF THE "GOLDEN CITY" BAZAAR
div.p: A VIEW OF THE "GOLDEN CITY" BAZAAR

as historic ground—(applause)— and the very last time he had the pleasure of meeting Mrs. Lloyd-George, just about a fortnight since in London, they were in historic precincts too, because thanks to the kinduess of Mr. and Mrs. Lloyd-George, his wife and he were invited to go into their old house in Downing-street and see the very chambers where SP many Chancellors of the Exchequer had prepared their statements. They were shown the very room and the very desk where in the early seventies Mr. Glitdstone prepared those famous financial statements that were the admiration of the whole coentry and he (Mr. Crosfleld) was sure all in that assembly were expecting that 14 ithin a few weeks they would have another very important, serious and

COURAGEOUS BUDGET which might no less be the admiration of all true well- wishers of their country to-day. (Applause). Alluding to the historical sketch contained in the bazaar hand- book, Mr. Crosfield said that while the most general knowledge of history must teach them the immense value to attach both*to toleration on the one hand and peace on the other, the history of Nonconformity did so in a very special degree. (Hear, hear.) He spoke relatively because, after all, everything in this world, not even barring the multiplication table,was relative. They did not want to get 'id of all competition, for healthy rivalry for pre-eminence in the artistic, intellectual and literary worTds, and, also on our athletic fields, was to be encouraged. It was the extreme view the other way to which he for 'one would never lend himself, and against which we had always to be upon our guard. He could not forget how only ten sears ago one heard quotations of a very unfortunate line in Tennyson about "-the blood-red blossom of war" and the tendency to stagnation that was-apt to be created in times of peace. As sears went on he believed we should value more rather than less the great principle of toleration. " Let us," said Mr. Crosfield," be tolerant in all things, except when we have to deal with what is despicable or mean. Holding pretty strong views of this kind on the question of peace, friends of mine in Warrington 'may ask : Why is it you voted the other day an the House of Commons (as I did unhesitat- ingly vote) for the Government's programme toincrease NAVAL. ARMAMENTS. Why are you as anxious and keen as anybody in War- rington to see this great Territorial undertaking made a success ? My answer to that is that I have a very deep conviction that taking the world as a whole and looking facts in the face, the influence of the British Empire is a great influence for good, and it is our duty not only as English patriots but as citizens of the world to see that that Empire is adequately defended. I allude to the topic to-day only because it is being made a burning—somewhat to.) burning a topic at the present ,time. I have fortunately during the last fortnight had opportunities in London of con- sulting a number of people who are experts i both n the Admiralty and in the Army and of getting a gcod deal of intimate and competent advice, and I am thankful to be able, to as4ured every- body in this room and every friend of mine in Warrington too, that our defences are in a magnificent condition and that there is no ground whatever for panic. When you luar of us in the House of Commons discussing what is called the two-power plus 10 per cent standard it is well to bear in mind that what we have at the present day is not a two-power but between a three and four power standard. When we know -also by the best expert advice that can be obtained that not only to-day but in 1911 and in 1912 our overwhelming power on the water will be immeasurably superior to that of any other power in Europe' I submit that in face of facts like that, we may well keep our heads cool and not lend ourselves to any of this -
WITH MRS. LLOYD GEORGE (inset).

—in fact that she was what they in Lancashire called "Jannock." (Laughter.) What they had seen and heard that day confirmed the impressions they bad formed. Mrs. Letheren also included in the Vote of thanks Mr. Crosfleld to whose interest and intercession she said they owed the presence of Mrs. Lloyd-George. That was not the first time they had reason to be indebted to him. Quite recently he had assured them that their Women's Circle had his sympathy. " I have faith in Mr. Crosfield as a politician " said Mrs. Letheren " but I am quite sure some of the ladies here won't have my reason for liking him as a Member of Parliament. It is because he has no intention of giving women the vote, at least for twenty.yeArs." (Laughter and applause.) The vote was enthusiastically accorded. Mrs. Lloyd-George, in acknowledging the com- pliment, said she was grateful to the m embers of the chu ch aid to the representatives of the Women's Liberal Association for their Leautiful flowers, She again hoped they would have a very successful bazaar. (Applause). The business of the bazaar then commenced.

div.head: MANUFACTURED A G ITATION
div.p: MANUFACTURED A G ITATION

which is being got up in London and which, I must say is sadly and unfortunately exaggerated. (Applause.) Mr. Crosfleld went on to say that those who were responsible for the conduct of affairs were neither negligent nor ctreless, but vigilant, and were taking thought not only for the present but for the future. That of itself might fill them with gloomy thoughts if they bad only that to look to, but what inspired them with hope was that the progress in the direction of arbitration, as a substitute for NS ktr, did not cease, and that in the long run, perhaps not for same ,decades yet, he feared, but in the fulness of time it would put an end to the barbarous arbitrament of NS ar between the white peoples of the earth. (Applause.) That could not be soon, and they must not forget that one of the greatest of Nonconformists' Old Oliver Cromwell, said "Trust in the Lord, but keep your powder dry." We had to keep our powder dry for many a decade yet, and he was afraid the time when strife between the different coloured populations of the globe would be ended too, was still more distant. But be was thankful that the principle of arbitration was making progress and be had faith to believe it would continue to do so. (Applause). Mr. Crosfleld con- , eluded by congratulating the earnest workers who had arranged that beautiful bazaar and said he bad the utmost pleasure in asking Mrs. Lloyd-George to declare it open. (Applause). • • Mrs. LLOYD GEORGE, who was greeted with loud applause on rising to speak, was then presented with two lovely bouquets by Mrs. B. Few on behalf of the church committee and Mrs. Osborne on behalf of the Women's Liberal Association respectively. Addressing the assembly, Mrs. Lloyd George said : It has given me very great pleasure to come here this afternoon to help in a good cause. I came, es you have heard, at the request of Mrs. Crosfleld and also of your genial and most popular member, Mr. Crosfield. (Applause). I have been looking at your handbook and find that yon as a church have been working steadily year by year and doing a very good work, and that now you have come to the conclusion that you can work better when you have finer.buildings. I also find that you are of good faith, for you put the high figure of £l,OOO to be raised for these new buildings. The work of the bazaar has been taken up by every section of the church —men, women, and young people—and that in iteelf is a good and healthy sign that you have the true elitist ian spirit here. I also saw in the handbook when I first opened it, familiar names such as Jones—(laughter)— Roberts, Lloyd,Williams,ete.—(laughter)--and I at once came to the conclusion that they were all of my nationality, and your minister has told you that your secretary is a Welshman. I am -Very pleased to see them amongst the forwards,for they would not be true representatives of their country it they did no religious work. We in Wales have been brought up from our childhood to take a very keen interest in the

div.head: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS ,--
div.p: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS ,--

The bazaar was re-opened on Thursday afternoon by Mr. Jas. K. Slater, ex-moderator of Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist churches. Mr. Henry Roberts presided and was supported on the platform by the Revs. R.E. Letheren, John Yonge, Hector V. Thomas and J. S. Ilugees. The CHAIRMAN said he hoped with all his heart that in spite of not particularly pleasant weather and of the very unfortunate conditions of trade in Warrington, the bazaar would not suffer unduly, but that all those who had a desire to help a church which bad fought its way ' against adverse , circumstances for so long a period end was now making a splendid effort to lengthen its cords and strengthen its stakes might receive the support of those who were not members of that church but who were kindred with tiara in spirit end in sentiment—Nonconformists like themselves and himself. He claimed that public work of a certain character might be made the band-maid of the greater work of the Christian Church itself and tbat any man who entered public life in that spirit, who might feel that he was not particularly called or had not the particular faculty necessary to do the more direct work of religious effort, might do as good and important a work in the sphere of public life if he addressed himself to it in the right spirit. (Applause). Mr. J. K.Slater said he had completed his 39th year as treasurer of the ToxtAh Tabernacle, Liverpool. Mr. Roberts was a Congregationalist, but he must admit that the Baptists were the first church ; the Congrega Vonalists came in a few days afterwards. (Laughter). If they read the first- and second chapters of the Acts they would find that the Btptists were in the fore- front. The late Rev. Hugh Price Hughes said Baptists ought to be proud because they were ever in the fore- front in their advooacy of civil and religious liberty and in their adherence to the fundamental truths of the Christian :religion. If that were true of the Baptist Church in Warrington, it was right that they should have premises worthy of the denomination. The Baptist and other evangelical denominations were more than ever needed at the present time, when they thought of the inroads of sacmn3entarianism and sacerdo- talism and of the presumption of priestism. They believed that all true believers in Jesus Christ were, priests unto God and they claimed that all who loved ' the Saviour mere truly priests and offered up their sacrifices to God every day of their lives. Therefore he hoped that Baptists, Congregationalists and other Nonconformists, and the Evangelicals in the Church of England would be true to the teaching of God's word in holding up Christ as the Saviour. Mr. CLA.TWORTHY announced that the takings the previous day amounted to £ll2 and that, including donations of £B5, the total was roughly £2OO. The Rev. HECTOR V. THOMAS, secretary of. the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptist Churches i moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. Slater.• He said one of the things we were suffering from in public life to-day, was the lack of willingness on the part of good and prominent Christian men to take prominent positions in municipal life. To remove the corruption that was prevalent, to uplift ideals that were so low, to cleanse and purify them—a better work than that no man in the church or out of it could put his hand to. He was glad they had a gentleman in the chair that day who had been made first of all a Christian citizen and now wanted to promote the Kingdom of God in the high office he held. Mr. E. WYNNE JONES seconded, anl the vote was heartily passed. Uy to Thursday evening the proceeds totalled ab3u t £270.

div.head: YESTER DAY'S (PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: YESTER DAY'S (PROCEEDINGS.

Yesterday afternoon the bazaar was re-opened by Mr. James Dodds. Mr. Norman Balmford presided and was accompanied on the platform by Mr. and Mrs. James Dodds, the Revs. R. E. Letheren and E. B. Keel!ng, Alderman Bennett, Mr. J. Longland, Mr. A. S. Elliott and others, The Rev, R. E. LETHEREN, while confessing to a sense of disappointment with the results io far achieved, said the third day always brought luck. (Laughter). Their friend Mr. Dodds had not left them in any doubt as to what he was going to do, for he had at once given them £5O. (Loud applause). They had therefore every reason for hopefulness. i welcoming Alderman Bennett, Mr. Letheren made an appreciative reference to a recent poem from his pen which appeared in the "Examiner," and said it was conceived in the spirit of true poetry. The CHAIRMAN said there was no church in which Ire had a closer or deeper interest than Golborne-street, for the reason that it was a Baptist Church and also becauss of old associations which would not easily be forgotten. He hoped that the congregation would rally round their leaders and not rest content until they had put the finishing touches on that great effort by seeing their new church erected and paid for. If theyall stuck to their posts and supported their enthusiasts, their joy would be sufficient reward. (Applause.) Mr. DODDS said that for many Years he had felt that. the great Baptist Church deserved to have a bettor position in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He knew something of their Church. As a .boy he was brought up in the village of One of their'great ministers, Dr. Wm. Landels—one of the finest and noblest men he

ever met—and that early association had always given him a great respect and admiration for the whole Baptist Church. Then when he (Mr. Dodds) was in London he used to listen to Charles Haddon Spurgeon, and to-day his voice seemed to thrill him as he thought of it. Many other good tnen he had known in different parts of the country, were connected with the Briptist Church. He felt, continued Mr. Dodds, that we wanted something representative of militant Nonconformity in Warrington. He believed it would be better for all kinds of Christianity if we had more of it. We wanted men of independence, of religious enthusiasm for good Causes, even if they were not popular—and be had felt that in Warrington we had-not had sufficient of that. The people whom they had to oppose respected them more if they were faithful to their principles, and willing to stand by them before all corners and in all places. He hoped that effort would succeed, and that they would have in Warrington by and by a strong Baptist Church. (Applause.) He had admired the brave and courageous work of Mr. and Mrs. Letheren, and he had been particularly delighted. with the way in which Mrs. Letheren h a stirred up various activities in Warrington. He hoped they might both be long spared and that the people of War- rington who could help Mr. and Mrs. Letheren would see to it that the work they had in hand was brought to a great success. Mr. Dodds made a feeling allusion to the late Mr. John Fieldhouse, a good Baptist, whom he always admired for his quiet Christian character. In conclusion he said that whether they raised the necessary £l,OOO or not, be knew they would struggle on with unfaltering will and undiminished faith, believing that the result was sure to come, and before long. (Applause). . Alderman BENNETT, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Mr. Dodds;' remarked that his grandparents on both sides were Baptists and for that reason, if for no other, he had always had a very friendly feeling towards the Baptist Church. It was pleasant to feel that the mem• hers of the various Free Churches were drawing closer together as the years went by and were beginning to feel that the things that divided them were very trivial, whereas the things that united them were very great and important. He hoped that would become increasingly so amongst all the Christian churches, because the existing divisions, want of charity, and misunderstandings seemed to be utterly contrary to the spirit of the great Master Whom they professed to serve. He did not agree with Mr. Dodds on many things, but everyone must be agreed as to his extreme goodness of heart and large minded generosity, a pleasing illustration of which had been given that clay. Mr. ELLIOTT in secon :lug said Mr. Dodds had given them the" sovereign remedy" they were requiring. The vote was cordially pas.,ed. THE ENTERTAIN NIEN TS.

A strong feature of the bazaar is the mrpst, inviting series of entertainments in which many of our, b est- knoctn local artistes appear. The promoters are to be congratulated on having secured such a 'splendid array of talent, and those who have not already been present at the entertainments should certainly make a paint of attending this (Saturd tv) evening. They will not be disappointed. Mr. Feed Fieldhouse and Mr. Edgar Balmford have had the direction of the concerts and already several high-clas3 programmes have been sub- mitted. The artistes who have kindly placed thheir ser- vices at the disposal of the organizers of the bazaar are: Sopranos, Mrs. C. Garton Stone,tMiss Emily Taylor, Miss D. Truslove, Miss S. Silcock ; contraltos, Madam Lily Fairhurst, Miss L. Plinston, Miss J. Armstrong ; tenors, Mr. J. Rabbitt, Mr. J. Draper, Mr. _S. Hassall,

Mr. A. Greenough.; baritones, Mr.. J. B. Poole, Mr. Fred Fieldhouse Mr. F. Bailey; basses Mr. J. W. Bibby, Mr. Wallace Ray, Mr. H. Plumplon ; enter- tainers and humorists, Mr. H. M. Ashton, Mr. E. .1. Sanders, Mr. Walter Moores; solo violin, Mr. Brad- ford Barton; solo violoncello, Mr. Edgar Bs.lmford ; pianists and accompanist;, Miss Millwood, Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac„ and Mr. G. W. Weaver.—The items include songs, duets, quartettes, instrumental solos and trios and humorous sketches. In addition there have been two bright and varied entertainments each evening by the pupils of Lorne House School, the first consisting of the Kinderspiel or juvenile cantata " Playmates " and the second of the operetta "Fairy match girl," the action song Chinese Lantern" (which secured the prize at the Warrington Musical Festival,") "The Girton girl "and " Milkmaid," by senior girls. Thanks are due to Miss Lloyd Williams, ;who arranged these very pleasing programmes, and to Miss. Roscollor, the actompanist. There are numerous side attractions, including a fish pond, baker's oven, shooting gallery, hall of laughter, the " Golden City" marionettes, Dutch auctions cqn-
ducted by Mr. ben Few, and various interesting competitions. There is also a smoke room ,ahere "worshippers of the weed may burn their idol."
THE PROCEEDS.

work must neutralise any advantage gained by the cheapening of commodities. Competition for work has driven the worker to accept the lowest possible wage subsistence. It has drivea the agricul- tural labourer to accept his 12s. a week. It has forced the town's labourer to accept his 17s. 7d. par week. The difference in these figures alone proves my case. Why should the agricultural labourer receive ss. a week less than the town's labourer? The answer is, because the cost of subsistence is about that much less in the country than in the town. Wherever we look, facts refute Mr. Parker's theory. To say that landlordisraa and capitalism would not tike advantage of the temperance of the people is to con- tradict history. They have already done so. The degree of temperance practised by the people is nigh criminal. These two forces have compelled everything to conform to their laws. They have compelled us to send our children and wives to work for their profit. And a monstrous social order that will d ) this, will not hesitate to confiscate any benefits that efficiency due to temperance may produce. One shudders to think of what mightthave been but for the interference of Factory Acts and the efforts of organised labour. As one of Shakespeare's characters says. " He owns my life, that owns the means whereby I live." The land- less man, the man without capital, is at the mercy of those who have. In order to live at all he has to bee leave to apply his labour to the land and capital owned by the landlord and capitalist. And to say to this man efficiency in production benefits him seems to me to be bordering upon the ridiculous, and I still assert that the consumer (the people) will not benefit by efficiency due to temperance or anything else so long as the means of production are owned and controlled for the benefit of a few. Thanking %Ir. Parker for his courteou s letter and the" Examiner" for its space allowed to mo —I am yours for Temperance and Efficiency.

div.head: Stockton Heath Choral Union.
div.p: Stockton Heath Choral Union.

Sir,—ln the account of our concert last 'week, you omitted to mention a most important item—the accom- panist, Mrs. Pendlebury, who has assisted the choir from the commencement, and has rendered splendid ser- vice. At the concert Mrs. Pendlebury accompanied on the piano, a most arduous task, and the soloists, band, and choir, are grateful for the help rendered. Allow me to mention that our Society le purely non-sectarian. Many people seem to think we are a part of the Wesleyan Church'. This is entirely a mistake. We only rehearse in the schools, and have absolutely no connec- tion with any denomination. The choir at present has members from tint Church of England, Catholics. Congregationalists, Wesleyans, etc., our sole aim being the cultivation of music and no questions of religion are asked. If people did not attend a church, we should admit them if they had good voices.—Yours sincerely, H. BERREY, Conductor to the Stockton Heath Choral Union.

div.head: Temperance and Efficiency.
div.p: Temperance and Efficiency.

Sir,—Although in disagreement I must congratulate Mr. Parker upon the higher tone and stronger argumenta- tive force of his fast letter, over his previous effusions. TO clear the field a little, it would be as well to say now, that I do not believe with the Tariff Reformers, that-the demand for labour is a "fixed limited quantity." My contention is that the call for labour can be increased by a more just distributiorrof wealth, by handing over unearned incomes to the producers of them. But the point debatable at present is, whether efficiency due to temperance will increase the call for labour. Mr. Parker's letter last week supported the assumption that any /efficiency in production cheapens the com- modity produced and the consumer- gains the difference, and its seems to me the result obtained from this controversy depends upon this point. The simplest and ifiest method of analysing this statement would be, I think, to compare the con- dition of society to-day and the time previous to the introduction of any mechanical efficiency worth speak- ing about. Let us took backwards, say, about 150 years or so and suppose for the moment the people of that period are reduced to the lowest level possible of material need, and then consider the progress made in the efficiency of production from that period until to-day. If Mr. Parker's theory be right, there should have been a steady increase of the material welfare cf the people until to-day we should have been living in exuberant luxury. Paradoxical as it may seem to be we have it upon the authority of Prof. Thorold Rogers that 400 years ago the general standard of life was higher and hours of labour shorter. He cAtimates that the everage family lived in compara- tive comfort with a labouring period of from about three to five months yearly. The state of affairs to-day has been so much dinned into our ears that it scarcely needs repetition from me. Suffice to say that at least one half (20 millions) of our population do not get so Relent to keep them up to a reasonable standard of physical efficiency. Facts prove just the opposite to Mr. Parker's-contention upon this point. But supposin,, he was right where does it lead us? Mr. Parker asserts that tile demand for labour depends upon the purchasing. power of the consumer and that competition regulates that power, which may be enlarged by efficiency in pro- duction, but he seems to forget there is also competi- tier) for employment which also must lower the purchasing power of the consumer. If the purchasing power of the consumer is increased, competition for
