div.head: What is Warrington's Dramatic Taste?
div.p: What is Warrington's Dramatic Taste?

Sir,—During the past week Warrington haS. had offered to it some of the very best plays ever written in the Englrsh language at the Royal Court Theatre by the F. R. Benson Shakespearean Company, and not only have such plays been offered, but the exposition of them by Mr. Henry Herbert and his talented company has been made in so artistic and so intellecteal a style, as I consider ought to have attracted all students of Nature and those interested in the higher abausement and education of the people. On Monday night Shakespeare's Comedy of "The Merry Wives of Windsor " was beautifully played in all its frolic, and although the first act lacked somewhat of proper pronunciation by some of the players, yet in the remaining acts it was produoed as well as it could be desired. Mr. Herbert's ponrtrayal of Sir John Falstaff was most admirable, his by-play and his rendering of the words were of the very highest order, and created roars of well-deserved laught4r and applause, and be was most capably assisted by three or four of his company. • Anyone going on Tuesday night, as I did again and seeing him in Hamlet,that prince of parts in that prince of plays,could hardly believe that it was the same actor. I have seen some of the most eminent players enact the part of Hamlet during my dramatic experience com- mencing with Barry Sullivan in the Old Band-Box Theatre in Scotland-road and subsequently by Henry Irving on his ever memorable production of Hamlet at the Lyceum Theatre, agd by Forbes Robertson and others, but I can without hesitation say that Mr. Herbert's rendering of Hamlet was equal in his elocu- tionary parts to any I have ever seen. It was a literary and intellectual treat, and all the members of his com- pany were admirably suited to their respective parts. How _delightful it was to listen to his Soliloquy of

. - "To be onot to be." Not a syllable of the whole could possibly be missed, but I was disappointed that he did not include the scene of Hamlet's address to the players. Again on Wednesday night we were treated to another phase of Mr. Herbert's versatility in his render- ing of " Shylock "in the" Merchant of Venice." His elocution and acting especially in the Trial Scene,were such that we marvelled at the change from Sir John Falstaff. I do not, however, consider his " Shylock "

was equal to his Hamlet, but he was most ably assisted by his company, more especially by "Antonio," whose idea of the character was beyond all praise. Miss Vanderzee gave the well-known "The quality or mercy is not strained " in a most attractive manner,and all the rest of the players were admirably suited to their parts. Yet with all these elocutionary and enjoyable pro- ductions what were the audiences to greet them ? On Monday night only a very moderate house, on Tuesday night it would have been the same except for the presence of the Training College Students who by their presence set off the auditorium, and on Wednesday night only again a moderate house, although the whole three productions were worthy of crowded audiences, who would have learned some wholesome truths. I am told and sincerely believe that Mr. Beech9m's instructions to his manager, Mr. Loader, are that only the best companies are to be engaged whenever they can be obtained, but unfortunately all in the dramatic business know that good companies with good pieces annot be secured for every week. Are the present houses for such a Company as we have had this week the slightest encouragement to Mr. Loader to continue his instructions? I trow not, and I can only add that Warrington ought to be ashamed of itself in not giving a heartier support to the present engagement. If the plays had been some absurd comic opera or . . .
so-calledmitsical comedy (save the mark!) the theatre would have been packed by a certain class of Warrington inhabitants, and on the other hand if the play had con- _ .

slated of some 25 characters at the cinnitencement, whose members had been reduced either by murder, an explosion, or other ultra-extraordinary means to the small five or six remaining alive at the end, the place would also have been, crowded by a different section of the public. Alas for the taste of both these classes ! I hope however Mr. Loader, backed by Mr. Beecham, will continue to bring to Warrington euch companies and such players as he has up to now been able to engage under the new management.—'Yours truly, ARTHUR BROWNE.
Warringt on. 26th March, 190 D.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

A nicely-varied programme is provided this week for the patrons of the Palace and Hippodrome. One of the brightest turns seen for some time is that submitted by Bellew and Stock's Company of juvenile entertainers known as the Eleven Romps. The title is somewhat of a misnomer, for these charming young ladies indulge more in singing and dancing than romping. There are some good vocalists among them, and the whole troupe is very smartly turned out. Bert Weston proved a very popular comedian, and his racy style of story and song greatly pleased the, audience. If encores had been possible in the time,Weston would have had to respond. Ted Karno and Co. presented a screaming absurdity entitled the "Dinner Hour," which consisted largely of the generous use of the slop-stick and rapid appearances and disappearances through doors in the trick scenery. Turns or this description seem to us a little out of date, and deficient in real humour. A clever and original juggling act is performed by the Cromwells, of whom the lady is exceptionally dexterous and earns rounds of applause. Dancing of a weird and wonderful kind is the special line of the Czar troupe, who certainly set a pace that the uninitiated would hardly care to follow. Charles Woodward sings topical songs in good voice, and Maudie Forde combines singing and sand-dancing in effective fashion. The orchestra and the biograph as usual contribute their quota to the entertainment. THE FIRST "SHAW" PLAY AT WARRINGTON.

Warrington playgoers flocked in large numbers to the Palace and Hippodrome on Thursday afternoon when, through the enterprise of Mr. Macnaghten, they had their first opportunity of witnessing a play from the pen of that unique dramatist, Mr. G. Bernard Shaw. There was a flying matinhe by Miss Horniman's Company of "Widower's Houses," a play in three acts which, we May say at the outset was brilliantly acted, and aroused great enthusiasm. The Shaw subtlety and satire were evident from the first line, almost, and if many people did not altogether grasp the inner meanings of "Widowers' Houses" they vastly enjoyed the smart- ness of the play and its vivid characterisation. The ethics of getting money form the theme, and Sartorious is strongly condemned by the hero, Dr. Trench, when the latter learns that his pro- spective father-in-law m tintains his position by screwing money out of half-starved tenement dwellers. Eyentu• ally, however, Trench finds that he is largely dependent himself on the interest of a mortgige on these same tenements. The inevitableness of struggling against present-day conditions of existence individually eventu- ally proves too much for Trench, who has in the end to take Blanche, the daughter of Sartorious,from the effects of an overpowering love and a despairing conscientious- ness. Mr. Shaw is possibly preaching the necessity for a grand reform of the social order, but at any rate his sermon is illuminated in a way which appeals even to the least thoughtful. Mr. Jules Shaw makes a remarkably clever study of the part of the grasping Sartorions whose redeeming feature is his love for Blanche. Mr. Lewis Casson as Dr. Harry Trench is excellent and is the high-principled but 'rather weak doctor to the life. Mr. Charles Bibby as Cokane, the tactful, suave man of the world, does his share in helping in the success of the piece, while Mr. Maxwell Harvie as Veccheese is very fine both in poverty and riches. Miss Mona Limerick plays Blanche very charmingly, though a little apt to overdo the emotional scenes. The minor parts are in the bands of Miss Louis Holbrook, Mr. Gerard Wynne and Mr. Leonard Mudie.

WARRINGTON UNION. CHILDREN ACT, 1908. Part. I. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that where a person resident within the Warrington Union area under- takes for reward the nursing or maintenance of one or more infants under the age of seven years, apart from their parents, or having no parents, for a period of more than forty-eight hours, he or she shall within forty-eight hours from the reception of any such infant, give notice thereof in writing to me. Where a person undertakes for reward the nursing and maintenance of an infant already in his care with- out reward, the entering into the undertaking shall, for the purposes of this Part of the Act, be treated as a reception of the infant. Where at the commencement of this Act any infant is under the care of any person who has, before the commencement of this Act, undertaken its nursing and maintenance under such circumstances that if the nursing and maintenance had been undertaken after the commencement of this Act he would have been required to give notice to me, he shall, within one month after the commencenhnt of this Act, give notice in writing thereof to me. • The notice shall state the name, sex, and date and placerf birth of the infant, the name arf the person receiving the infant, and the dwelling within which the infant is being kept, and the name and address of the person from whom the infant has been received. Theprovisions of this Part of this Act shall not extend to any relative—grandparents, brothers, sisters, uncles, and aunts, and, in the case of illegitimate infants the persons who would be so related if the infant were legitimate—or to any person who undertakes the nursing or maintenance of an infant under the pro- visions of any act for the relief of the poor, or to hospitals,convalescent homes or institutions established for the protection and care of infants,and conducted in good faith for religious or charitable purposes, or boarding school at which efficient elementary education is provided. The Act comes into force on the Ist April, 1909. A copy of Part I. of the Act and al k information con., cerning same may be obtained from me on application. By Order, Bewsey Chambers, ARTHUR BOTTOMLEY, Warrington, March 2:ith,1909. Clerk.

BLACKBURN PHILANTHROPIC BURIAL SOCIETY. Chief Office :—King-street., Blackburn. Local District Office, Carlton House Chambers, Sankey-street, Warrington. SUMMARY OF THE ANNUAL REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET for the year ending December 31st, 1908. In common with most other kindred institutions, particularly those having a large amount of business in Lancashire, the Society has suffered materially by the general depression in trade and commerce that was the bitter experience of the major portion of last year, but notwithstanding this, the premium income was increased by the sum of £s,7o3,roaking the income from premiums alone for last year £97,001, as compared with £54,385 for 1891 The total income was £113,493. The claim rate was P 46 per cent. of the premium income less than the experience of 1907, although the number of claims paid, i.e., 4,876, and ambunt, £42,785 Os. 5d., are greater than those of 1907 by 13 in number and £1,187 17s. 81d. in amount. This makes the sum paid in claims during the last 13 years into £429,756. The Society's funds, which are the property of the members, were increased during the year by the unpre- cedented amount of £36,132 Os. id., making the same, at the end of the year, £479,203 4s. 33d., or nearly FIVE times the annual premium income, a fact that FEW, if any, other offices can boast of, and which ought to give the utmost confidence to members and the public generally.
